text:
Hello, my wonderful young explorers, and welcome!

I'm Uncle Andy, and just like you, I absolutely love discovering the amazing secrets of our planet! For over four decades, I've been fascinated by the magic of nature. Seeing green forests calms my heart, and every animal, big or small, fills my mind with wonder and curiosity!

I've been lucky enough to travel to incredible places, from the sunny lands of Mexico and the beautiful countries of Europe, to the bustling wilds of Asia, where I lived for over fifteen years. I'm even a teacher! But my biggest wish was always to share the incredible stories of the natural world with curious kids just like you.

So, I wrote these books! I hope you'll enjoy reading these adventures and learning about amazing creatures as much as I loved exploring and researching them. Get ready to imagine every leap, every sound, and every secret hiding place!

Now, let the adventure begin, my young explorers!

"Here we are," mumbled Sunny the Capybara, her whiskered snout nudging a juicy clump of pond grass. "Another truly beautiful day in my personal wonderland."

The golden sunshine danced on the shimmering surface of the lake, and the little frogs hummed a sleepy tune while bigger frogs joined in with deep, rumbling croaks, creating a beautiful morning orchestra. In the background, Sunny and her family listened, occasionally adding their own soft whistles as they munched on sweet watergrass. Sunny herself even gave a gentle whistle, a tiny tune, as the brave little bird landed softly and delicately groomed her broad, flat back. She just blinked her kind, brown eyes, enjoying the gentle tickle.

"Ah, it's the perfect time for grazing!" Sunny sighed, a contented rumble deep in her chest, as she glanced up at the fluffy white clouds drifting across the wide, blue sky. "It looks like it might rain later, but for now, it's glorious."

Once Sunny had finished her delicious breakfast of tender grasses and sweet water lilies, she began to think about her next task.

With a happy splash, Sunny waddled towards the lake's shallow edge. She wasn't alone, not at all! Her big, bustling family and many friendly capybara cousins were already busy, collecting all sorts of yummy water plants. Together, they gathered crunchy cattails, leafy water hyacinths, and more juicy reeds.

"We need to hurry!" Sunny gently called out to the others, her voice a soft, rumbling bark. "The rain is coming, and I still need to take my morning nap!" She looked up at the sky, seeing cumulus clouds, puffy and fluffy like giant pieces of popcorn, tumbling slowly across the blue. She paused, then added with a happy sigh, "You see, Capybaras like me absolutely love napping right in the cool, refreshing water to stay nice and fresh! It's the best way to beat the heat and relax!"

While the rest of her family and friends kept busily gathering their food, Sunny felt the midday heat starting to prickle her fur. "It's getting warmer and warmer," she sighed, looking for a way to cool down. Her whiskers twitched, and her nose found just the spot – a small, refreshing puddle of cool, soft mud!

"Ah, finally, some relief!" Sunny mumbled happily as she gently eased herself into the silky, cool goo. The mud squished around her, coating her from head to paw. This little muddy haven was just for her. No chattering birds flew overhead, and the frogs kept their distance. "It's so peaceful here," she whispered, closing her eyes. "Now I can truly take my morning nap, even if the rain is coming later." Sunny stretched out, feeling the cool mud soak into her skin, and soon drifted off to sleep.

During Sunny's wonderful, relaxing nap, the fluffy, popcorn-shaped clouds she had seen earlier had crept closer. They were now directly overhead, no longer looking like a tasty snack but growing darker and grayer. Then, a soft 'plip, plop' sound started. Tiny, cool raindrops began to fall, landing gently on Sunny's whiskers and nose.

"Ohhh!" Sunny mumbled, stirring slowly. "I guess my nap is over!" She stretched lazily, feeling completely refreshed and wide awake. "But it was a good nap! I feel so cool now!" she whispered, slowly emerging from the delightful mud puddle. Her eyes blinked open, wide and curious. "But now... I'm hungry again! And there's nothing I like to eat in this mud. Time to move back!"

As Sunny squelched out of her muddy bath, the temperature began to feel much more comfortable. The sun, though still bright, was gentler now. She looked towards her group and smiled. "Look at them!" she whispered to herself. Most of her big family were resting peacefully in the shade of the tall water plants, or half-submerged in the cool lake. "They look so cute!" Sunny thought. "I think they decided to rest because of the rain, just like me. Capybaras often rest in the water or under thick plants during the day to keep cool and safe!"

As Sunny squelched back to her group, the gentle rain began to fall a little harder. The hidden frogs seemed to love it, singing even louder from their watery hiding spots! One by one, Sunny's family started to stir, gently touched awake by the cool drops and the lively frog chorus.

"I'm back!" Sunny cheerfully announced, her voice a happy bark that helped wake the last few sleepy capybaras who were still trying to snatch another moment of rest. Her wide, hungry eyes scanned the green plants. "I hope you saved some yummy greens for me!"

Under the light of a big, bright moon, the capybaras began to munch on the delicious plants they had gathered. It was a peaceful scene of quiet munching and soft whistles.

Suddenly, a loud, sharp whistle pierced the night! It came from a bigger capybara, calling everyone to reunite. Danger was near! A group of shadowy crocs were hunting, moving closer to their peaceful spot. Sunny didn't waste a second. She was smart, and she knew it was time to hide!

"Everyone, listen!" Sunny whispered urgently. "I saw a nice, big, muddy puddle not far from here. I think we'll be much safer there!" She was right – the thick mud helped them blend into the murky ground, making them harder for the crocs to spot. "Let's grab a few more delicious plants, we still have a tiny bit of time!"

Moving swiftly as a group, grinding their leafy greens, they followed Sunny under the moon's silvery glow. "The moon will guide us," Sunny murmured, "and soon the big clouds will help us too, hiding the moon so we're extra safe." They slipped into the muddy place, disappearing beneath the tall, dense vegetation.

The crocs swam past, unable to smell their hidden dinner. The capybaras were safe for another day!

"Ohhh, what a beautiful but exhausting day," Sunny muttered, still munching on her greens, feeling full and content. "Another day is gone, but a new one will start soon!"

The moon was finally covered by the clouds, casting shadows over the hidden capybaras. Safe and sound, some kept eating, while others, already cozy, drifted off to sleep, dreaming of tomorrow's sun.

“Hrrumph!” Echo announced, lifting her enormous nose out of the river. A little egret jumped in surprise. “Good morning to you too!” Echo chuckled. The African sun was already painting the water gold, and her family lay in the shallows like a collection of enormous, rather sleepy stones. Only their eyes, ears and nostrils showed above the surface. Echo liked to call this her river hat.

The egret was searching for breakfast along the bank. Every time a ripple arrived, its reflection broke into a hundred little pieces. Farther downstream, behind a bend thick with reeds, the water was almost perfectly still. Echo watched the bird step into the sheltered shallows. “A quiet corner in a noisy river,” she murmured. “I wonder why the waves never seem to reach it?”

A dragonfly drew a brilliant blue line across the water, then landed on a reed. Echo tried to follow its reflection with her nose, but her own little ripples broke the picture apart. She stopped moving. Slowly, the river became a mirror again. In the quiet bend, the egret could see straight down to the little fish in the shallows. Echo watched until the bird caught one with a quick jab. How much easier everything seemed when the water was still!

Her mother called her back to the family. Echo pushed off the riverbed with her strong feet, bouncing through the water rather than swimming like a fish. “Coming!” she grunted. Hippos spend much of the hot day in water to protect their skin and keep cool. Echo settled beside her mother, flicked a fly away with her ear and closed her eyes. The little bend slipped out of her thoughts.

By afternoon the wind had arrived. Whoooosh! It shook the reeds and sent little waves slapping against Echo's cheeks. “My river hat is getting rather uncomfortable,” she complained. Then she heard a different sound: a tiny, worried peep. On a low branch near the bank stood a young egret. Its mother had flown around the bend, and the youngster seemed unsure where to go.

The young bird took a step along the branch. It was a very thin branch indeed, and when a gust swept down the river, it bounced like a spring. Echo's ears twitched. She could hear the larger birds calling over the water, but the little one's voice was almost swallowed by the wind. “I have a very big mouth,” she thought. “Perhaps a very big shout would help?” She opened it, then hesitated. The youngster already looked frightened enough.

Echo wanted to hurry over and help. She took one enormous step, sending a wave rolling towards the branch. The little bird flapped in alarm. Echo froze. “Oh dear. Perhaps enormous feet are not always the answer.” She backed away slowly. Her mother watched from nearby. “Give the little one some room,” she advised. Echo nodded, although doing nothing felt terribly difficult.

Then a familiar white shape appeared between the reeds. It was the mother egret! Echo remembered the quiet corner from breakfast. She could hear the mother's calls whenever the wind softened. The youngster turned its head, but another gust made it crouch. Echo waited quietly with her family, hoping the wind would settle before darkness arrived.

Echo found a comfortable spot a little upstream from the branch. Each time one of the other hippos shifted, she felt the water stir against her belly. She wondered how the same little wave must look to a bird with feet as thin as twigs. She resisted the temptation to make another splash and watched the reeds instead. Between two gusts, the quiet voice came again. The little bird lifted its head. This time it seemed to know which way to look.

As the sun sank, the waves became smaller. The mother egret called again. This time the youngster answered, spread its wings and fluttered towards the sheltered bend. Echo held perfectly still. A moment later two white heads appeared above the reeds. “There you are!” Echo whispered, delighted. She had not needed to carry anyone or make a single enormous splash.

The hippos began leaving the river to graze on land, as hippos often do after sunset. Echo followed her mother towards the fresh grass. “I thought helping meant doing something big,” she admitted. Her mother gave a soft grunt. “Sometimes the kindest thing is to make room for someone else.” Echo considered this while chewing a particularly delicious mouthful.

As she grazed, Echo discovered something rather funny. The loudest sound on the bank was not her enormous voice at all, but the ridiculous chomping noises her own family made. She tried chewing silently and lasted about three seconds. Her mother gave her a sideways look. “Being quiet when it matters is quite different from being quiet forever.” Echo swallowed her mouthful and laughed. She liked being a noisy hippo. She liked knowing when not to be one, too.

The stars appeared one by one. From the quiet bend came a final little call, and Echo answered with a gentle rumble. She imagined the birds settling safely among the branches. Her own family was close, the grass was sweet, and the evening air felt wonderfully cool. “Goodnight, little voices,” she murmured. The river carried on its soft, endless song.

“To-kay! To-kay!” Click gave one last call before the sun climbed over the garden wall. The spotted gecko had spent the night hunting insects, and now his favourite wooden beam was waiting for him. He climbed upside down without a wobble. Tiny structures on his toe pads helped him grip the surface. “Who needs a staircase?” he whispered, squeezing into his shady hiding place.

Tap, tap, tap! Click opened one eye. A long leaf outside the window was brushing the glass whenever the breeze blew. He watched it carefully. When the breeze stopped, the tapping stopped too. “A leaf with a very important announcement,” he decided.

Before settling back to sleep, Click inspected the leaf from his beam. It was green on one side, pale underneath, and it turned over like a little door every time the wind came through. He counted the taps on the glass. Two, then four, then nothing at all. “That is a very strange sort of conversation,” he thought. Unlike a gecko's call, the tapping always came from exactly the same spot. He remembered that detail before his eyelids grew too heavy to keep open.

He listened for a little longer, then tucked his tail comfortably beside him.

A younger gecko named Dot lived behind a nearby beam. Dot was still learning the sounds of the garden and had a habit of answering everything, even the squeaky door. Click heard a tiny chirp from Dot's hiding place. “Time for sleep,” he murmured. Tokay geckos are mostly active at night, so both neighbours disappeared into the cool shadows as the morning grew brighter.

In the afternoon, rain drummed on the roof. Click woke when a particularly large drop struck the window. Tap, tap! Dot chirped from behind the other beam. Tap, tap! Dot chirped again. Click blinked. Was Dot having a conversation with the leaf? He peeked out just far enough to see the wet garden shining below.

Dot edged towards the end of the beam, peering into the dripping garden. “Perhaps the other gecko has lost its way,” came the little voice. Click could understand the worry. Once, when he was much smaller, the sound of a broom brushing the wall had made him hide for an entire evening. There was nothing silly about a sound you didn't understand. He watched Dot's tiny toes grip the wood and decided to turn the mysterious tapping into a game.

“Hello? Are you there?” Dot called in their imaginary gecko language. The leaf answered with another tap. Click almost laughed, but then remembered how strange the garden had seemed when he was young. He did not want to embarrass his neighbour. “Listen for a moment,” he called softly. A gust rattled the leaf three times, then everything went quiet.

Dot waited. No answer came until the next gust. “That's funny,” Dot whispered. Click explained what he had seen in the morning. “The wind is moving a leaf. It isn't another gecko.” Dot was disappointed. Click promised that the garden would have plenty of real voices once darkness fell. For now they returned to their sheltered resting places.

“Let's make a prediction,” Click suggested. “When the next gust comes, watch the leaf.” The two geckos waited. A raindrop rolled down the glass, and a wet branch bent towards the window. Tap, tap, tap! Dot's eyes widened. “It moved before the sound!” Another gust brought exactly the same result. Dot gave a small, delighted chirp. The mystery had been solved not by guessing louder, but by looking closely. Even a rather boring leaf had turned out to be interesting.

At dusk, the rain stopped and insects gathered around the garden lights. Click emerged, stretched his toes and called, “To-kay! To-kay!” From a distant tree came a real answering call. Dot listened in astonishment. It sounded quite different from the tapping leaf. Then a moth fluttered past, and Click caught his supper with a quick movement.

Dot gave a little chirp of excitement. “I think I know the difference now!” Click smiled. The two geckos explored their own safe corners of the wall, leaving each other plenty of space. Dot even noticed a beetle moving before Click did. “Excellent listening, neighbour!” Click said. Dot looked very pleased indeed.

A faint buzz rose from beneath the lamp, and Dot turned towards it before anything was visible. A beetle appeared on the wall, its tiny legs ticking against the plaster. Click was impressed. Dot's careful listening was already useful for hunting, and there were plenty of insects for both neighbours to explore separately. From somewhere in the darkness came another deep tokay call. Dot stopped to listen, then looked at the leaf. “You can keep tapping,” the youngster told it. “I have other things to hear now.”

The moon rose above the wet garden. The leaf tapped once more, and this time Dot did not answer. Instead, the youngster gave a tiny amused chirp. Click settled into a sheltered crack for a short rest before his next nighttime hunt. He thought about how much there was to discover when you stopped and listened. Outside, the garden whispered its many different songs.

Mimi opened her eyes in a square of golden sunshine. She stretched one paw, then another, until she looked almost twice as long as an ordinary cat. “A very successful morning,” she purred, although she had done absolutely nothing yet. From the other side of the room came a little jingle. A kitten was batting a soft toy with a bell sewn securely inside it.

The kitten gave the toy one enthusiastic whack. It rolled under the big armchair. Jingle, bump, silence! Mimi peered underneath. She could see a little corner of the toy beside the chair leg. “How rude of you to hide,” she told it.

Mimi took one more look. The smell of the toy was still on the rug. Mimi followed it with her nose until she reached the edge of the armchair, where a rather dusty fluff ball was pretending to be something interesting. She gave it an experimental pat. It stuck to her paw. “An entirely useless clue,” she muttered, shaking it away. The kitten watched from behind her, ears pricked. Then her ears pricked at the sound of bowls rattling in the kitchen.

Her human called the cats for breakfast, and Mimi decided that a proper detective should never investigate on an empty stomach.

After breakfast, Mimi washed her face with a damp paw. The kitten chased a patch of sunlight across the floor, forgetting the missing toy for a while. Mimi noticed that the armchair had a wider opening at the back than at the front. She sniffed it, flicked her whiskers and climbed onto the windowsill. A warm nap seemed much more urgent than detective work.

In the afternoon the kitten began searching everywhere. It looked in its basket, beside the curtains and even underneath Mimi's tail. “Excuse me!” Mimi protested. The kitten gave a miserable little meow. Its favourite toy was missing. Mimi remembered the morning's jingle and led the kitten towards the armchair.

The kitten had tried to entertain itself with a crumpled piece of paper, but the paper did not jingle. It had tried a ball, but the ball did not feel quite right. Mimi suddenly remembered the first toy she had ever loved: a little fabric mouse that had been almost as big as her head. She had carried it everywhere. She looked at the kitten again, and the mystery no longer seemed like an amusing way to pass the afternoon. It was somebody's very important treasure.

She reached under the front with one paw. Nothing. She tried the other paw. Still nothing. Her whiskers brushed the narrow sides when she leaned closer. Cats use their sensitive whiskers to gather information about nearby objects and spaces. Mimi decided not to squeeze herself into the gap. “A detective must keep her whiskers in excellent condition,” she announced.

Then she remembered the opening at the back. She walked around the chair, crouched and reached in from the wider side. Her paw touched something soft. Jingle! The kitten bounced with excitement. Mimi hooked the edge of the toy and pulled it slowly into the light. But just as she did, she discovered how wonderfully it rolled across the floor.

The bell made a cheerful sound, and Mimi's paws seemed to have minds of their own. Before she knew it, she had chased the toy halfway across the rug and stopped it neatly between her front feet. What a splendid toy! The kitten followed, then sat at a polite little distance, with its tail curled around its paws. Mimi looked down at the prize. She had done all the work of finding it. But the kitten had been waiting all day for this moment, too.

Mimi gave the toy a gentle tap. Jingle! She tapped it again. The kitten watched, waiting. Mimi could have played with it all evening, but she remembered the kitten's sad little face. She nudged the toy towards its owner instead. “Your turn, little detective.” The kitten pounced, rolled over and landed with all four paws in the air.

Their human joined them for a little supervised play, rolling the toy across the rug. Mimi discovered that watching the kitten's ridiculous leaps was almost as entertaining as chasing the toy herself.

For the first time that afternoon, the kitten was so busy playing that it forgot to look sad. It pounced on the empty rug, missed the toy completely and gave an offended little meow. Mimi rolled onto her side, unable to resist joining in. Their human made sure the game stayed gentle, and soon two shadows were bouncing across the carpet. The kitten was purring even as it waited for the next turn.

When the game ended, their human put the toy away for another day. The kitten climbed into its basket, then changed its mind and snuggled beside Mimi.

Outside the window, the last sunlight disappeared. Mimi listened to the kitten's tiny purr, which sounded rather like a miniature motor. She had found something more enjoyable than keeping a treasure all to herself: making someone else happy. She tucked her paws beneath her chest, and the two cats drifted off like two warm little loaves of bread.

Bruno woke to a wonderful smell drifting through the kitchen. Toast! Unfortunately, the toast belonged to his human. Bruno had his own breakfast, which he ate with the enthusiasm of a dog who had not eaten for approximately a hundred years. In reality, it had been since yesterday evening. After breakfast he trotted outside, ready for his morning inspection.

At the garden gate he discovered a glove lying beside a patch of mint. Bruno sniffed the glove, the mint and a rather uninteresting stone. Dogs can gather an extraordinary amount of information through their noses. This glove smelled familiar. He carried it back to his human, who laughed and thanked him. Bruno wagged proudly. Another mystery solved!

Bruno conducted one final inspection of the garden before declaring it ready for the day. There was the mint, the patch of damp earth beneath the tap, and the very important corner where a squirrel sometimes appeared. Each place had its own story of smells. He heard his human laugh behind him. “What a busy nose!” Bruno lifted his head proudly. If somebody ever needed a garden detective, he was quite certain that he would be the first dog they called.

A little puppy called Pip was visiting that day. Pip chased a butterfly while Bruno investigated a strange rattling sound. Every time the wind blew, the garden gate shook. Bruno tilted his head. The latch looked different from usual. His human was nearby, hanging washing, and Bruno went over to sit beside her. Then Pip dropped a yellow ball at his feet. Inspection time was over, apparently.

By afternoon, the wind was blowing harder. The washing danced on the line, and Pip bounced after the yellow ball. Bruno lay beneath a tree, enjoying the shade. Suddenly there came a familiar sound. Rattle, rattle, click! The gate had opened a little. Beyond it was a pavement where people and bicycles sometimes passed. Pip had spotted another butterfly.

The gap at the gate was only a little wider than Pip's head, but the puppy was very small. Bruno could hear the thin whir of bicycle tyres beyond the fence. His tail stopped wagging. The butterfly was doing what butterflies always did, wandering wherever it liked, and Pip was following it without noticing anything else. The garden suddenly seemed much too quiet. Bruno looked towards the house. His human was busy inside. How could he get her attention and persuade Pip to turn around at the same time?

Bruno sprang up. The puppy was heading towards the opening, his little ears flapping. Bruno wanted to race after him, but running outside would only put both dogs in danger. Instead he barked loudly from inside the garden. His human turned towards him. Pip paused for a moment, then looked back at the butterfly. Bruno needed something more interesting than a butterfly.

The yellow ball! Bruno remembered how much Pip loved it. He picked it up and trotted away from the gate, towards the house. Then he dropped it and nudged it across the grass. Pip heard the familiar bounce and spun around. Suddenly the butterfly was forgotten. The puppy bounded after the ball, tumbling over his own enormous paws. Bruno barked again to attract his human's attention.

Bruno kept the ball near the house, far from the opening. He rolled it once more, and Pip pounced so enthusiastically that the ball bounced under his chin. Bruno gave another sharp bark towards the kitchen. This time he heard footsteps. He stood between the puppy and the gate without trying to chase either the butterfly or the bicycles. Pip, delighted by the game, dropped the ball at Bruno's feet. “You found me!” his expression seemed to say. Bruno gave him a friendly sniff. Yes, he certainly had.

Their human hurried over and secured the gate. She checked the latch carefully and moved the dogs inside while she arranged to have it repaired. Bruno received a gentle pat. Pip received a drink of water and a quiet place to rest. He had no idea why everyone seemed so relieved. He was simply delighted that his favourite ball had returned.

Later, with the gate safely fixed, the dogs enjoyed a supervised game in the garden. Pip tried to carry two toys at once, which was rather difficult with such a small mouth. Bruno watched him drop one, pick it up and drop the other. Even a great detective could not solve that particular problem. He settled beside his human, feeling pleased with the day's work.

When the gate was closed again, Bruno gave it a very serious inspection from a safe distance. No rattle, no click. Their human tested the latch herself and thanked Bruno for making such a fuss. He was rewarded with a scratch behind the ears, exactly where he liked it best. Pip settled down with the yellow ball and began licking it as though it were the finest dinner in the world. Bruno thought about the butterfly. He had not caught it. He had not even left the garden. Yet his little adventure had ended rather well.

As evening arrived, Pip curled up beside Bruno. The older dog had discovered that courage did not always mean rushing into danger. Sometimes it meant staying safe, thinking carefully and calling someone who could help. Outside, the wind had become a gentle whisper. Inside, two sleepy tails lay still, and two happy dogs dreamed of a garden full of yellow balls.

Rosa greeted the morning with a long, musical moo. The meadow was sparkling with dew, and the grass tasted especially delicious. A young calf named Clover was already bouncing around her mother. She leapt over a tiny clump of grass as though it were a mountain. Rosa watched with amusement. Being young, she decided, must be a very tiring occupation.

The herd wandered towards a hedge. Rosa noticed a broad patch of shade beneath a tree, where a little breeze slipped through the leaves. Nearby stood a water trough that the farmer had filled. She took a drink and listened to the birds. Clover was busy chasing her own shadow. “You'll never catch that one,” Rosa mooed. Clover tried anyway.

A small bird perched on the fence and sang three bright notes. Clover tried to imitate it, which produced something halfway between a moo and a hiccup. Rosa lifted her head in amusement. The shade beneath the tree was so pleasant that Rosa decided to stand there a little longer. The leaves made moving patches of light across her back, and the trough was close enough for another drink. Clover, who still had a great deal of morning energy, hurried back to her game. She barely noticed the cool spot.

As the sun climbed, Rosa settled down to chew. Clover stared at her. “But you haven't picked any more grass!” she exclaimed. Rosa explained that cows bring partly digested food back to their mouths to chew it again. This is called chewing the cud. Clover tried to imagine eating breakfast twice and decided that cows had a rather excellent arrangement.

By afternoon the meadow felt very different. The dew had disappeared, and the sunshine was strong. Flies buzzed around the herd. Rosa flicked her tail and walked slowly towards the hedge. Clover had been playing with another calf, but now her leaps were smaller. She stopped beside her mother, looking tired. The games no longer seemed quite so exciting.

The meadow seemed to shimmer in the distance. Clover looked at her playmate, then at a flower she had been trying to jump over. It was such a little flower. Why did the jump suddenly seem like such a big effort? She tried one small bounce, stopped, and leaned towards Rosa. “I don't feel like winning anymore,” she admitted. Rosa didn't tell her to try harder or finish the game. She gave a soft moo and looked towards the tree. There was a much better place to be on a day like this.

Rosa remembered the cool place she had discovered that morning. She walked towards it, and Clover followed her mother. The farmer had checked the water trough and made sure it was full. Clover drank, then stood in the shade beside Rosa. A breeze moved through the leaves. “Even the wind is taking a little rest here,” Clover murmured.

For a while they did nothing at all. Rosa chewed her cud, and Clover watched a beetle making its way across the ground. The beetle climbed a blade of grass, slipped down and began again. Clover giggled. She had been so busy racing around that she had never noticed how much was happening in one tiny patch of meadow.

A ladybird landed beside Clover's hoof, its tiny red back shining like a polished apple. Clover watched it unfold its wings and fly away. For once she had no wish to follow. A breeze passed through the leaves above them, and she took another comfortable drink from the trough. Rosa could see that her calf was beginning to relax. “The meadow hasn't gone anywhere,” she said. “It will still be here when the air is cooler.” Clover rested her head beside her mother. Perhaps an afternoon could be lovely without a single race.

When the farmer came to check the herd, the cows were resting comfortably. Clover was feeling more like herself. She wanted to run back into the sunshine, but Rosa remained in the shade. Clover decided to stay with her mother a little longer. There would be plenty of time to play when the afternoon became cooler. Even the beetle had disappeared beneath a leaf.

As evening approached, the herd returned to graze. Clover walked beside Rosa, stopping now and then to investigate interesting smells. She spotted her shadow again, stretching long across the meadow. This time she did not chase it. “You can come with me,” she told it. Rosa gave a soft moo that sounded suspiciously like laughter.

The other calves were enjoying the cooler air now, and one of them invited Clover to play. She agreed to a short game, then chose to stop when she felt tired. Her friend stopped with her and together they watched a grasshopper leap. It was astonishing how far a creature with such tiny legs could go. “Perhaps we should let him win today,” Clover suggested. Rosa listened to their happy noises from nearby. Her little calf was learning to notice more than the finish line.

The sky turned pink, and the meadow filled with the quiet sounds of insects. Clover nestled close to her mother. She had learned that looking after herself was not a waste of playtime: drinking, resting and noticing how she felt helped her enjoy the day. Rosa closed her eyes for a moment. The grass would still be there tomorrow, and so would the games.

Pippo woke to a most peculiar sight: a feather was floating past his nest, standing straight up like the sail of a tiny boat. He hurried down to the pond, tripped over his own webbed feet and landed with a magnificent SPLASH. His sister laughed. “Excellent entrance, Captain Pippo!” she called. Pippo bowed, which was rather difficult while floating.

The feather sailed towards a patch of reeds. Pippo paddled after it, watching how the water curled around the stems. Behind them was a quiet little pool, almost completely hidden from the rest of the pond. He could hear the wind above him, but the water here hardly moved. “A secret harbour!” he whispered. His sister was more interested in breakfast.

Pippo circled the sheltered pool. A water beetle drew tiny rings on its surface, and the tall reeds made a kind of green fence between him and the rest of the pond. He could still see his family through the opening, so he didn't wander farther. The feather came to a stop beside a leaf. Pippo gave it a little nudge with his bill. “You are a remarkably clever boat,” he informed it, although the feather, being a feather, did not seem particularly impressed.

They dipped their heads beneath the surface to search for food, their bottoms pointing towards the sky. A frog watched from a lily pad. “Are you two upside down on purpose?” he croaked. Pippo emerged with a dripping beak. “Of course! That's how professional ducks eat.” He shook himself, and droplets rolled off his carefully preened feathers like little silver beads.

By afternoon, clouds were gathering. The breeze pushed the floating feather across the pond much faster than before. Pippo tried to race it, but every time he drew close, another gust sent it spinning away. His mother called the young ducks together. “Stay near me, everyone. The wind is getting stronger.” Pippo reluctantly abandoned his race.

As the family gathered, the pond changed colour. The pale clouds turned grey, and little dark ripples chased one another towards the bank. Pippo watched his feather vanish behind a wave and appear again a moment later. His brother was trying very hard to keep up, paddling so quickly that the water bubbled behind him. Pippo's favourite race suddenly looked much less amusing. He wondered whether the feather would disappear entirely, and then wondered something more important: where could the ducks rest until the wind grew quieter?

A sudden shower rattled the leaves. The ducks were quite comfortable in the rain, but the open water was becoming choppy. Pippo's smallest brother, who had been paddling happily all morning, was struggling to keep up. “My legs feel like two cooked noodles!” he complained. Pippo slowed down beside him, while Mother Duck gathered the rest of the family.

Then Pippo spotted something white bobbing near the reeds. It was his feather! He remembered the sheltered water behind them. “Mother, there's a quiet place over there!” he called. Mother Duck looked carefully and led the family towards the opening. Pippo stayed beside his brother, matching his little strokes instead of racing ahead as he usually did.

They reached the reeds just as another gust swept over the pond. Pippo felt the waves pushing from behind, but Mother Duck was already leading them into the calm opening. The water changed almost immediately. His brother gave a little surprised quack. “It's still raining, but the pond has stopped bouncing!” The feather bobbed against a reed like a tiny flag. Pippo waited until the smallest duck was safely beside the others before he went to look at it. There was room here for the whole family, not just the fastest swimmer.

By evening the rain had softened to a gentle patter. Inside the sheltered pool, the ducks floated comfortably together. Pippo's brother stretched his tired feet. “You could have won your race,” he said. Pippo looked at the feather resting against a reed. “I think I found something better than winning.” His sister grinned. “Captain Pippo and his secret harbour!”

When the wind finally settled, Mother Duck led everyone back towards their resting place. The pond reflected the pink clouds, and the frog was still sitting on his lily pad. Pippo told him about the adventure. “So you discovered a harbour by chasing a feather?” asked the frog. “Exactly,” said Pippo. “Very important scientific duck work.”

The frog puffed up his throat and made a tremendous croak, as if he were announcing Pippo's discovery to the entire pond. Pippo's sister giggled. She had spent the morning thinking the feather was rather boring, but now she wanted to see the hidden pool on another calm day, with Mother close by. Pippo agreed. The feather drifted past them once more, and this time nobody raced it. They let their little boat sail wherever the breeze decided to take it.

The family settled together as the stars appeared. Pippo tucked his bill into his feathers and listened to the last little ripples. He had discovered that paying attention to small things could help someone else, and that staying together mattered more than being first. Somewhere among the reeds, his little feather floated quietly. Goodnight, Captain Pippo. The pond was peaceful again.

Oli opened one eye and discovered a leaf resting on his nose. He opened the other eye. The leaf was still there. “A very small roof,” he announced to his mother. High in the rainforest canopy, their sleeping nest rocked gently among the branches. Mother stretched her long arms, and Oli copied her, almost poking himself in the ear.

Breakfast was a delicious collection of ripe fruit. Oli reached for a fig, but a broad leaf above it caught his attention. Rainwater from the night before rolled down its smooth surface and dripped neatly off the pointed tip. He held the leaf over his head. “Look! No drips!” Mother smiled and showed him how to hold it without tearing it.

Oli turned the leaf over and examined its strong central rib. The water travelled along the green surface instead of soaking straight through. He tried a much smaller leaf, which protected exactly one eyebrow. Then he tried the large one again. Mother patiently watched his experiments while she finished her fruit. The rainforest was full of useful things if he remembered to look at them. A leaf could be breakfast for one creature, a hiding place for another, and, apparently, an excellent roof for an orangutan with a very wet nose.

They travelled slowly through the trees, testing branches before trusting their weight to them. Oli wanted to swing straight across a wide gap, but Mother chose a safer route through neighbouring branches. Along the way they passed a sturdy fork in a tree, surrounded by thick leaves. Oli thought it looked like a splendid little room with green walls.

In the afternoon, the forest grew unusually dark. Thunder grumbled far away, and the birds became quieter. Oli was investigating a delicious-looking fruit when the first enormous raindrop landed on his forehead. PLOP! He looked up indignantly. “Who threw that?” Another drop landed on his nose. Mother began moving towards a more sheltered part of the canopy.

Oli could no longer hear the little birds he had been listening to that morning. Instead, the canopy creaked and shivered around him. Water ran down his reddish fur and dripped from the ends of his long fingers. He gripped a firm branch and stayed near Mother. The gap they had looked at earlier was almost invisible behind the curtain of rain. Oli did not like the idea of crossing it now. He searched the trees for something familiar. Wasn't there a strong fork in one of the branches they had passed?

Oli remembered his little roof and picked a large leaf. It kept some rain off his face, although his furry elbows were soon wet. He giggled at his reflection in a puddle of water caught in a branch. His hair was sticking out in every direction. “I look like a very surprised pineapple!” Mother waited while he adjusted his leafy umbrella.

The wind began shaking the smaller branches. Oli noticed that the route ahead looked rather exposed. He pointed towards the sturdy fork they had passed that morning. Mother examined the branches and led him back along the safer route. Under the thick leaves they found a sheltered place to wait. Oli held his umbrella above his head, feeling very pleased with his discovery.

From their sheltered perch, Oli watched the water race down the trunks. His leaf umbrella was beginning to sag. He adjusted his grip, exactly as Mother had shown him, and the rain slid harmlessly off one side. Mother had chosen a much stronger shelter than any leaf could provide, but Oli's little invention made waiting there more comfortable. A bright green beetle crawled beneath the edge of his roof. “Another customer!” Oli whispered. He moved his hand slightly to leave room for his tiny visitor.

By evening, the storm had passed. Droplets sparkled on the leaves, and insects began their familiar chorus. Oli and Mother continued through the canopy, finding a few more fruits before settling down. He offered Mother his battered leaf. It had a hole in the middle and looked rather like a green doughnut. She accepted his gift with a gentle touch.

Mother began bending branches and arranging leafy twigs into a fresh sleeping nest. Oli helped by bringing a handful of soft leaves. Some landed in the nest; others landed on his own head. He watched carefully as Mother tucked the branches together. One day, he thought, he would be able to build a wonderful nest all by himself.

Oli tried to copy the way Mother bent a branch into the nest. His first attempt sprang back, leaving him holding only a leaf. His second stayed in place, although it was rather crooked. Mother showed him where to tuck the end, and this time his little piece of the nest held. Oli gave it a delighted pat. It felt good to make something useful instead of simply watching. The storm had taught him to look carefully, and the evening had given him a chance to practise what he had learned.

As the forest darkened, Oli snuggled beside Mother. Today he had learned that clever discoveries begin with noticing ordinary things, and that learning from someone experienced is nothing to be ashamed of. His leaf umbrella lay beside him, its work finished. Far below, the rainforest whispered and rustled. Oli closed his eyes beneath his much bigger roof of stars and leaves.

Tiko woke beneath a curtain of green leaves. His mother was stretching her enormous paws, and he decided to stretch his too. Unfortunately, his back paw caught a twig. CRACK! A startled bird flew away. “I meant to do that,” Tiko announced. Mother blinked slowly. Tigers have excellent hearing, and Tiko was beginning to discover just how many secrets the forest could tell him.

They walked through tall grass where sunlight painted golden stripes across the ground. Tiko looked down at his own black stripes. When he stood still among the shadows, even his tail seemed to disappear. Mother showed him how to place his soft paws quietly. He tried three careful steps, then sneezed. A butterfly fluttered away, apparently unimpressed by his magnificent tiger skills.

A tiny patch of sunlight moved along Tiko's shoulder as the leaves swayed above him. When he shifted into the grass, his mother seemed to disappear too, even though she was only a short distance away. Her stripes broke up the outline of her body among the stems. Tiko decided to test his own disappearing trick. He crouched very still, until a ticklish blade of grass touched his nose. His magnificent hiding place ended with another sneeze. Mother looked at him, and Tiko was sure she was smiling.

Suddenly something rattled beside a fallen log. Tiko crouched and wiggled his bottom. “A mysterious forest monster!” he whispered. But Mother waited, and so did he. A little dry seedpod rolled into view, pushed by the breeze. Tiko laughed. He nudged it gently with his nose. Mother reminded him that a sound alone cannot tell you what is hiding nearby.

By afternoon the air was warm and heavy. Tiko followed Mother towards a shallow stream where they could cool themselves. Unlike many cats, tigers are comfortable in water. Tiko dipped one paw into the stream and splashed his own whiskers. He looked around to see whether anyone had noticed. Mother was already wading peacefully through the shallows.

The water felt lovely after the heat of the forest, and Tiko paddled gently in the shallow part near Mother. Farther along, the stream twisted around a bank covered with tall plants. A little piece of earth dropped into the water with a soft plop. Tiko watched the ripples travel away. Then a leaf slipped down the same bank. He was curious, but his mother was ready to leave, so he followed her. He did not know that the very same place would catch his attention again before the afternoon was over.

On their way back, another rustling sound came from the grass. Tiko almost sprang forward, but remembered his morning monster. He stopped and watched. A long branch was swaying in the breeze. Beyond it, the muddy bank had crumbled into the stream. The grass concealed the broken edge completely. His whiskers twitched. That would have been a very unpleasant surprise.

Mother was investigating a scent nearby. Tiko gave a soft call and waited for her. When she returned, he looked towards the broken bank. She sniffed the ground and turned towards a firmer route among the trees. Tiko followed, stepping carefully over roots. He felt rather proud that his patient little investigation had helped them avoid the slippery edge.

As they passed the firmer ground, Tiko heard the branch scraping once more. This time he could see where it moved against the edge of the bank. A little clump of earth slid away, leaving the grass leaning over the water. He looked up at Mother. The noise had not been a creature inviting him to play at all. The seedpod in the morning had been harmless; this new sound had been a useful warning. Two mysteries, two different answers. Tiko found that rather exciting.

As evening approached, the forest changed its tune. Frogs began calling, insects chirped and birds settled into their roosts. Tiko tried to identify each sound. One frog sounded remarkably like his own stomach. He decided that perhaps it was time for another meal. Mother led him deeper into the forest, where the shadows grew longer and their striped coats blended into the trees.

Later, they paused beneath a broad tree. Tiko practised his silent steps around a root. This time he managed to move without cracking a single twig. He was so delighted that he nearly announced his success at the top of his voice. Instead, he gave Mother a gentle nuzzle. She rested her chin near his shoulder, and he curled his tail around his paws.

A distant bird gave a short call, followed by a soft splash somewhere near the stream. Tiko lifted his ears, but he stayed comfortably where he was. There were hundreds of sounds in the forest, and he would never understand all of them in a single day. He decided to begin with the ones close to him: Mother's breathing, the wind in the leaves, the quiet tap of a falling seed. Before long he could hardly keep his eyes open. Listening, he discovered, could be wonderfully relaxing as well as useful.

Tiko thought about the seedpod and the hidden bank. Being quick was useful, but knowing when to wait was just as important. He didn't need to pounce on every mystery to be a wonderful tiger. For now, he could rest beside Mother before their next nighttime adventure. The forest whispered softly around them, and his golden eyes slowly closed.

Kiki woke to a chorus of birds in the rainforest canopy. She stretched her wings and admired her enormous colourful bill. “Good morning, breakfast!” she called to a cluster of ripe fruit. Her brother fluttered onto the branch beside her. Kiki's bill looked heavy, but its lightweight structure helped her reach fruit without carrying a great weight on her head.

The two young toucans hopped along the branches, choosing ripe berries. Kiki tossed one into the air and caught it neatly. Her brother tried the same trick and missed. The berry bounced off a leaf and disappeared. “Perhaps the forest was hungry too,” Kiki giggled. They continued until they reached a tree with a broad crown of thick, overlapping leaves.

From beneath the broad leaves, the canopy looked like a green ceiling. Kiki could hear water dripping from a plant high above them, but the branch under her feet was almost dry. Her brother hopped to one side and found a little sheltered perch. Their large bills helped them reach fruit that was difficult to get at from a branch, but even the finest bill could not make a flimsy twig stronger. Kiki remembered where the sturdy branches were. She was very interested in a nearby tree that still held several ripe figs.

Under those leaves grew a cluster of fruit that was not quite ripe. Kiki wanted to try one, but her brother suggested leaving it for another day. Nearby, they spotted a different branch with ripe figs tucked beneath the leafy roof. Kiki remembered the place. From there, she could see their family's tree hollow across a small gap in the canopy.

After midday, clouds gathered above the rainforest. The wind shook the branches, and raindrops began tapping the leaves. Kiki and her brother moved closer to the trunk of a sturdy tree. The rain grew louder until it sounded like a thousand tiny drums. Kiki tried calling over the noise, but her brother could barely hear her.

A particularly loud gust made the leaves turn their pale undersides towards the sky. Kiki held the branch and tucked herself close to the trunk. She had expected the shower to pass in a moment, but the drops kept coming. Her brother's stomach made a little sound. “Mine too,” she admitted. Their favourite feeding branch was somewhere beyond the wet leaves. She wondered whether the fruit there would still be waiting when the rain stopped. Then she remembered the broad crown they had visited earlier and the protected branches beneath it.

When the shower eased, they flew a short distance to their usual feeding branch. Several ripe fruits had fallen during the storm. Her brother looked disappointed. Kiki remembered the sheltered figs from the morning. She waited until the wind had quietened, then called to him and flew towards the familiar broad tree. The leaves were dripping, but the branch beneath them was still full of fruit.

Kiki reached for the largest fig. Then she noticed her brother struggling to reach one on a thin twig. Instead of eating immediately, she hopped aside and let him use the sturdy branch. He caught a fig and gave a delighted croak. They took turns reaching for the fruit. There was plenty for both, and neither needed to risk balancing on the slippery twig.

The fig was soft and sweet, and Kiki ate it with a little toss of her head. Her brother had found one of his own. From their sturdy perch they could reach another cluster without leaning out too far, so they moved along the branch together. A few seeds fell into the forest below as they ate. Somewhere, much later, a seed might find a place to grow. Kiki was not thinking that far ahead, however. She was thinking that a shared picnic was a great improvement on two very wet, very hungry toucans.

By evening the clouds had drifted away. Drops of water sparkled in the golden light. Kiki and her brother flew back towards their family's hollow, stopping to eat a few more berries along the way. Like many fruit-eating birds, toucans help forests grow by carrying and spreading seeds. Kiki had no idea that her breakfast might help a new tree grow somewhere far below.

At their resting tree, Kiki tucked her bill among her feathers. Her brother made one last attempt at tossing a berry and caught it perfectly. Kiki gave a cheerful little call. “Tomorrow you'll be teaching me!” she said. The two settled near their family as the forest grew quieter, listening to the last drops falling from the leaves.

The forest seemed to be drying itself one leaf at a time. A little bird called from a nearby branch, and Kiki answered with a soft croak. Her brother was still pleased with his successful berry toss. He offered her the next one, and she accepted it without trying to show him how much better she could catch it. They had each noticed something useful that day. Kiki imagined all the places they might discover together tomorrow, and then tucked her head into a comfortable position. There would be no need to rush breakfast.

Kiki remembered the fruit she had wanted to eat all by herself. Sharing the branch had made the afternoon much happier, and remembering a little detail had helped them both. She decided that tomorrow she would look for more wonderful places to explore together. Beneath the shelter of their tree, the young toucans grew sleepy. Outside, the rainforest shimmered under the evening sky.

The sun was barely above the grass when Ella woke to a very peculiar noise. Splosh! Her little cousin had tried to drink with his trunk and sprayed his own forehead instead. Ella laughed and showed him how to draw water into his trunk and pour it into his mouth. He tried again. This time he watered Ella's toes.

Grandmother led the herd away from the muddy pool towards breakfast. Beside the path stood a tall termite mound with a crooked top. “A birthday cake!” Ella announced. Grandmother explained that tiny termites had built it, and that the mound was a useful landmark on the way to another waterhole. Ella looked back twice, trying to remember its funny shape.

Ella tried to imagine the little termites building such an enormous mound. She could hardly see the tiny creatures, yet their home rose above the grass like a tower. Grandmother pointed out another landmark, a pair of trees with branches bent in different directions. Ella made up a little song: “Crooked cake, two funny trees, rocky hill and water, please!” Her cousin joined in at the wrong moment and made an enthusiastic trumpet. Grandmother waited patiently until they were ready to continue. Ella had no idea how useful her silly song might become.

The elephants pulled up grasses and reached for leaves. Ella used the little finger-like tips of her trunk to pick up a particularly delicious stem. Her cousin tried to copy her, but grabbed a dry twig instead. As they ate, Grandmother pointed out a distant rocky ridge. Ella wondered why grown-ups spent so much time looking at things that weren't lunch.

By afternoon the sun was hot enough to make Ella flap her enormous ears. Moving air over their ears helps elephants cool down. Her cousin was no longer bouncing along beside her. His steps had become slow, and his mother stopped to let him rest in the shade. The little pool they had passed earlier was now far behind them.

The herd moved slowly, their feet raising little clouds of dust. Ella noticed that the older elephants were no longer pulling at every patch of grass. They were looking ahead, searching for the familiar routes. Her cousin leaned into his mother's side and gave a tired little sound. Ella remembered his cheerful morning shower, and suddenly wished she could turn the whole sky into a waterhole. But she was still a young elephant. She could not make rain, and she did not know the way by herself. What could she remember that might help?

Ella wanted to rush ahead and find water herself. Then she noticed something poking above the grass: a crooked brown tower. Could it be the birthday cake? She moved closer to her grandmother and gave a low rumble. Elephants can communicate with deep sounds, some too low for human ears to hear. Grandmother turned towards her.

“Look, the termite mound!” Ella said. Grandmother recognised it immediately. She knew the route from there to a dependable waterhole beyond the ridge. The herd set off together at a comfortable pace. Ella walked near her cousin and his mother. Whenever the little one stopped, Ella stopped too. Finding water would be no good if they left someone behind.

Beyond the mound, Ella saw the two funny trees from her song. Farther away, the ridge rose above the golden grass. Grandmother had travelled this way many times, and she chose the familiar path rather than taking a shortcut across an unfamiliar patch of land. Ella matched the rhythm of the herd's footsteps. From somewhere beyond the ridge came a faint call of birds. Her cousin lifted his head. Ella hoped it meant water was close, but she waited for Grandmother to lead the way.

At last Ella smelled damp earth. Beyond the ridge lay a wide pool, shining in the late sunlight. The grown-ups checked the surroundings before the calves approached. Ella drank deeply, then splashed water over her back. Her cousin attempted another enormous spray. This time it landed right on Grandmother's dusty knee. Even Grandmother seemed amused.

As the air cooled, the elephants dusted their damp skin with loose earth. The coating helped protect them from the sun and insects. Ella asked Grandmother how she remembered so many places. “One journey at a time,” Grandmother replied. Ella looked towards the ridge and imagined all the paths she might learn as she grew older.

Ella tried her little song again. This time she added the pool and the place where they had found shade for her cousin. Grandmother listened, then reminded her that the same landscape could look different after rain or during another season. Remembering a shape was helpful, but experience taught elephants which places they could depend on and when. Ella leaned her head gently against Grandmother's side. She was glad she had asked for help instead of running ahead. There were many more journeys to learn, and she had an excellent teacher beside her.

When the stars appeared, the herd gathered quietly, with the little calf close to his mother. Ella felt proud, not because she had known everything, but because she had noticed something useful and asked someone who knew more. Her cousin leaned against her side. Tomorrow there would be more paths, more grasses and probably more accidental showers. Tonight, everyone had enough water, and Ella was happy.

Zuri woke with a leaf tickling her nose. She stretched her long neck and plucked it from the branch above her. Breakfast had practically delivered itself! Beside her stood a younger giraffe named Lolo, stretching so hard that his ears wobbled. The leaf he wanted remained just beyond his reach. “I think my neck forgot to grow last night,” he complained.

Zuri showed Lolo a lower branch with plenty of tender leaves. She curled her long tongue carefully around a leafy twig, avoiding the sharp thorns. Lolo copied her and chewed happily. From her higher position, Zuri noticed a row of trees stretching towards a sheltered clearing. She remembered the shape of the tallest tree, which looked rather like an open umbrella.

A small bird landed high in the umbrella tree and looked down at them. Lolo lifted his head until his ears pointed almost straight up. “Can you tell what it is doing?” he asked. Zuri could see it hopping between the branches, but she could not see the tiny insect Lolo had noticed beside his feet. They laughed. The tall view and the short view each had something interesting to offer. Zuri looked back at the shape of the umbrella tree before they wandered on. It stood out beautifully against the morning sky.

The giraffes wandered slowly across the savanna, browsing as they went. Lolo asked whether Zuri could see all the way to the moon. “Only if the moon comes down for breakfast,” she joked. Their mothers were nearby, watching the surroundings. Zuri enjoyed being tall, but she sometimes forgot that the world looked quite different to someone much smaller.

After midday a strong wind swept across the plain. Dry leaves rattled and dust rose from the ground. Lolo blinked and tucked his head close to his mother's side. The giraffes began moving away from the exposed grassland. Zuri could see the tops of the trees she had noticed earlier, although the dust hid much of the ground.

The dust made the familiar savanna seem as though somebody had rubbed an enormous brown pencil across it. Zuri could still see over some of the drifting dust, but when she lowered her head she understood why Lolo looked worried. The grass, the trees and even the giraffes' legs seemed to disappear and reappear. Lolo kept close to his mother. Zuri wanted to tell him that everything was perfectly fine, but she could see how uncomfortable the wind had become. Instead, she looked for the landmark she remembered.

There was the umbrella-shaped tree! Zuri stayed beside her mother as the adults moved towards the sheltered area. Lolo tried to hurry, but his long young legs seemed to have different ideas about which direction to go. Zuri slowed down beside him. “We aren't racing the wind,” she said. “It would probably cheat anyway.”

As they reached the trees, the wind became less fierce. Lolo was hungry again, but the first branches he found were too high. Zuri spotted a smaller tree a little farther along. She waited for the adults to move towards it, then showed Lolo the leaves within his reach. He took a bite and smiled. The dusty afternoon suddenly seemed much less troublesome.

The little clearing was not completely still, but the trees broke the worst of the wind. Zuri blinked the last of the dust from her eyes and watched Lolo pull a leaf from a low branch. His long, dark tongue curled around it rather neatly. “My neck did grow a little, after all!” he said proudly. Zuri laughed and chose a higher branch for herself. Neither had to struggle for the same leaf. Above them, the umbrella tree swayed like a very large parasol, and the afternoon began to feel comfortable again.

By evening the wind had softened and the sky was turning gold. Zuri watched Lolo discover a particularly tasty cluster of leaves. He called her over, proud of finding something himself. The leaves were low enough that Zuri had to bend her neck to reach them. “Your turn to stretch down!” he giggled. Zuri happily shared his discovery.

Their mothers continued browsing nearby. Zuri noticed that giraffes did not all need to eat from the same height. Young ones could reach different branches, and older ones could reach the taller trees.

Lolo found one more small cluster hidden among the lower twigs and called Zuri over. She bent down to see what he meant. From his height, the leaves were obvious; from hers, a broad branch had hidden them. “I would have walked straight past those,” she admitted. Lolo looked as pleased as if he had discovered an entirely new tree. Zuri decided that being tall did not make her the best discoverer of absolutely everything. She had a useful view, and Lolo had a useful view. Together they could notice far more.

She thought about the clearing and the little tree. Being able to see far was useful, but noticing what someone else needed was even more important.

As darkness approached, Lolo settled near his mother while Zuri stood quietly beside her own. The umbrella-shaped tree was now a dark silhouette against the sky. Zuri wondered what tomorrow might bring and what Lolo might discover before she did. Perhaps they would find another wonderful breakfast together. The breeze whispered through the leaves, and the savanna grew peaceful.

Ziggy was convinced that his mother wore the finest stripes in the entire savanna. One stripe near her shoulder curved like a little hook. He tried to find the same shape on his own coat, twisting around until he nearly bumped into another zebra. “Looking for your tail?” his mother asked. Ziggy grinned. “Looking for your favourite stripe!”

The herd grazed in the cool morning air. Ziggy noticed that every zebra had a different pattern, rather like the different shapes of clouds overhead. His mother explained that young zebras learn to recognise their mothers by their appearance, smell and voice. Ziggy listened to her familiar call and decided that he could recognise it anywhere, even with his eyes shut.

Ziggy tried to make a game of recognising the other zebras. One had a stripe shaped like a bent stick, another had a pattern that reminded him of a lightning flash. But when they began walking together, the patterns seemed to slide into one another like a moving picture. His mother called him, and he recognised her voice without looking. “That's much easier!” Ziggy announced. He trotted beside her, enjoying the familiar smell of her coat. The herd was full of lovely patterns, but his mother's was still his favourite.

A yellow butterfly fluttered past his nose. Ziggy followed it for two little steps before his mother called him back. He returned immediately and nibbled the grass beside her. The butterfly landed on a flower, opened its wings and flew away. Ziggy hoped he would see it again. There were so many interesting things to discover in the savanna!

In the afternoon the herd moved through a patch of taller grass. Ziggy spotted another yellow butterfly dancing above the stems. He watched it zigzag left and right, then turned to tell his mother about it. But the zebra beside him had a different shoulder stripe. He looked around. Suddenly all those black and white patterns seemed to be moving at once.

The butterfly seemed to have vanished into the grass. Ziggy turned one way and then another. A pair of striped legs passed in front of him, and another pair moved behind. He could smell the herd and hear the soft sounds of grazing, but the face he wanted was not immediately visible. For a moment he felt very small indeed. He wanted to dart between the adults, searching every stripe. Then he remembered how clearly he had heard his mother in the morning. Perhaps his ears could help where his eyes were finding things difficult.

Ziggy felt a little flutter inside his tummy, and it wasn't a butterfly. He remembered his mother's voice. Instead of running through the herd, he stopped beside the nearby zebras and called out. He listened carefully. A familiar answer came from just beyond two grazing adults. Then he saw a shoulder with a little hooked stripe moving towards him.

His mother reached him and touched her nose to his face. Ziggy breathed out a great sigh. He told her about the butterfly and how the stripes had become confusing. She stayed close as they continued through the grass. This time Ziggy watched the butterfly only while it was near them. When it disappeared, he let it go.

His mother gave him another familiar call, and Ziggy pressed his nose against her shoulder. The hooked stripe was right there, as wonderful as ever. He noticed that his heart was beating much more quickly than usual. His mother waited until he had calmed down before moving with the herd again. When the yellow butterfly returned, Ziggy pointed his nose towards it and called her attention to it. They watched it together. This time he was not the only one who got to enjoy the discovery.

Later the herd reached a shorter grassy area. Ziggy found a lovely flower and called his mother to look. A butterfly landed on it, and they watched together without moving away from the group. Its wings opened and closed like two tiny doors. Ziggy whispered that it must be getting ready for bed. His mother gave a soft snort.

As the sun sank, the zebras gathered together. Ziggy looked at the stripes of the other foals and imagined a grand parade, each wearing a completely different costume. He no longer thought his curiosity was a bad thing. It had helped him discover butterflies and flowers. He simply needed to remember where his family was while he explored.

A young zebra nearby had a little stripe like a crooked river. Ziggy pointed it out to his mother and then showed the foal the hooked stripe he loved so much. Soon the two youngsters were inventing names for the shapes they could see while staying near their families. “That one is a very wiggly banana!” Ziggy giggled. The evening grass smelled sweet, and the herd moved calmly together. Curiosity still felt like a wonderful thing, especially when there was somebody close by with whom he could share it.

Under the first stars, Ziggy rested close to his mother. He could see the little hooked stripe even in the fading light. Tomorrow he would find new things to admire, and perhaps he could show them to his family instead of wandering after them alone. He closed his eyes, listening to familiar voices and the soft rustle of grass. His favourite stripe was right beside him.

Tuga woke beneath a ledge where the sea was still blue and sleepy. She stretched one flipper, then another, and rose to the surface for a breath. Above her, a gull shouted as though it had invented the morning. “Good morning to you too!” Tuga called, before diving towards her favourite meadow of seagrass.

Breakfast was delicious, although Tuga suspected that nobody on land would agree. She was halfway through a particularly tender mouthful when a ribbon of seaweed floated past her nose. She watched it sweep around a rocky point, turn slowly and disappear into a little bay. How curious! The water seemed to have roads that nobody could see.

A little fish darted between the blades of seagrass and then vanished as neatly as if it had closed a green curtain behind itself. Tuga rested near the bottom for a moment and watched the drifting seaweed. On one side of the rock it travelled quickly; on the other side it turned in a slow circle. She rose for another breath, then looked down at the same rock from the surface. It was an excellent landmark, even in a world where the ground and sky seemed to move all the time.

Tuga followed the ribbon just far enough to discover a quiet patch behind the rocks. Tiny fish hovered there without being swept away. She surfaced, took another breath and memorised the shape of the point. Then she returned to breakfast. “An excellent morning,” she decided. “Two discoveries and at least seventeen mouthfuls.” She had lost count after twelve.

By afternoon the water was moving much faster. Tuga could see sand drifting along the bottom like smoke. Nearby, a smaller green turtle was paddling furiously towards the meadow but hardly moving at all. Every time he stopped to breathe at the surface, the current carried him farther away. His flippers were beginning to tire.

The young turtle tried another tremendous stroke. His shell moved forwards a little, then slipped backwards. Tuga recognised the look on his face. She had once become so determined to reach a favourite feeding place that she had forgotten to notice which way the water was carrying her. A piece of seaweed swept past them. Instead of fighting it, she watched where it went. There was the rocky point from breakfast, with a calmer patch of water on its far side. Could they reach it without struggling straight against the current?

“I'm going backwards!” he complained. “And I'm not even trying to!” Tuga knew the feeling. She began swimming towards him, keeping clear of the strongest flow. She remembered the ribbon of seaweed and the quiet bay. Perhaps they did not have to fight the water at all. Perhaps they could choose a different route.

She showed him how to move towards the sheltered side of the rocky point rather than straight against the current. They took their time, surfacing whenever they needed air. At last the water grew calmer. The little turtle stopped paddling and stared in surprise. “My flippers have stopped arguing with the ocean!” he said. Tuga laughed.

From the calmer water, the young turtle looked back at the sandy clouds swirling around the point. He could hardly believe they had been so close to a resting place all along. Tuga showed him another drifting leaf of seagrass, which turned gently instead of racing away. The two rose for a comfortable breath, and the little one finally relaxed his flippers. They waited until the conditions were suitable rather than trying to hurry back. A curious fish inspected their shells and then went about its own mysterious fish business.

As evening approached, the sand settled and the fish returned to their usual hiding places. The two turtles nibbled some seagrass while waiting for the current to ease. Tuga explained that she had discovered this place by watching a piece of seaweed. “A piece of seaweed taught you?” asked the youngster. “Well, it didn't say much,” she replied.

When the water became gentler, the little turtle could continue towards his familiar feeding ground. Tuga watched him disappear beyond the meadow, swimming steadily instead of frantically. She felt pleased that a small discovery had helped someone else. Being strong was useful, she thought, but noticing what was happening around you could be even more useful.

Tuga spent a few more minutes exploring the edge of the meadow. In the evening light, every blade of seagrass seemed to wear a little golden ribbon. A group of fish moved with the water and turned together when the current changed. Tuga thought about the young turtle's determined little flippers. They had been working so hard, and yet the water had been working harder. She was glad he had found a gentler route. Tomorrow she would probably discover another of the ocean's invisible roads.

The last golden light slipped through the water. Tuga took a final leisurely breath at the surface and settled beneath her familiar ledge, where she could easily swim up again. The sea whispered against the rocks. Tomorrow there would be more invisible roads to discover. Tonight there was nothing to hurry for, and Tuga rested her tired flippers.

Inky had eight arms and, according to Inky, at least nine excellent ideas before breakfast. Today his first idea was to find a new home. His old rocky den was comfortable, but a curious crab kept visiting the entrance and rearranging his shells. “I liked that shell exactly where it was!” Inky protested. The crab seemed unimpressed.

He slipped across the seabed, changing his colour to match the sand and stones. Under a broad rock he found a wonderful hollow. It had a front entrance and a narrow opening at the back. Inky squeezed through the little gap, using his soft body to fit where a much larger fish could not follow.

Inky inspected his new home with great seriousness. Four arms explored the front entrance, two examined the floor, and the remaining two seemed to have forgotten their instructions entirely. He pulled a small empty shell aside and tested the narrow gap once again. Because an octopus has no rigid skeleton like a fish's, his soft body can pass through surprisingly small openings, provided the hard beak fits. He decided the little doorway was not terribly elegant, but it might be useful. His eight arms approved, in eight slightly different directions.

He collected a few loose shells and placed them near the front entrance. Then he explored the back opening again. It led into a patch of seaweed that swayed gently in the current. “Two doorways!” he said happily. “One for arriving, one for leaving, and neither needs a doorbell.” He went out to search for breakfast.

In the afternoon, Inky was examining a crevice for small crabs when a large hungry fish appeared beyond the rocks. Inky flattened himself against a stone and changed his skin to blend with it. The fish swam past, then turned around. Inky stayed perfectly still. Even his most adventurous arm understood that this was no time for exploring.

The shadow of the fish passed over Inky's rock. He could see its fins moving in the blue water above him. For a moment the octopus considered making a dash for his front entrance, but the fish was between him and that part of the rock. Inky's skin matched the surrounding stone so closely that even the little pale speckles were difficult to distinguish. Still, hiding forever was not a particularly exciting plan. He needed to remember the shape of his den and the other way in.

When the fish moved away, Inky slipped towards his new den. But another fish was investigating the front entrance, attracted by the movement of a little crab nearby. Inky stopped behind a rock. He could not safely dash through the front door. For a moment he wished he had stayed in his old home, troublesome neighbour and all.

Then he remembered the narrow opening behind the den. He travelled around the rock through the seaweed, keeping close to the bottom. One arm found the gap, then another, and soon his whole soft body slipped inside. The fish outside continued searching without noticing him. Inky tucked himself into the hollow and waited quietly.

Inside the hollow, the water was dim and wonderfully peaceful. Inky peeked out just far enough to watch the shadow of the fish pass again, then withdrew into safety. His eight arms settled one by one around the rock. Outside, a little cloud of sand drifted away, and the fish finally turned towards another part of the reef. Inky waited a little longer before venturing out. “No need to open the door just because the visitor has gone,” he murmured. The reef would still be there when he was ready.

By evening both fish had gone. Inky peeped out, checked the water and ventured outside. The little crab from earlier was still hiding beneath a shell. Inky left it alone and found food elsewhere. He had already had quite enough excitement for one day, and the seabed offered plenty of other places to explore.

Back at his den, he admired the two entrances. He had not needed to be faster than every fish in the sea. He had needed to know his surroundings and choose wisely. “Nine excellent ideas,” he murmured, “but remembering one good idea is sometimes quite enough.” A tiny shrimp passed by as if agreeing with him.

Inky rearranged two empty shells near the entrance and admired his work. He was not building a grand castle, just making himself a comfortable little home. The narrow doorway, which had seemed like the least interesting part of his morning discovery, was now his favourite feature. A small crab crept past the rocks, and Inky's eyes followed it curiously. He had plenty of time for another little exploration before resting. For now, he was rather pleased to sit quietly in the place he knew so well.

The water darkened and the seaweed rocked gently outside his back doorway. Inky arranged his shells, curled his arms comfortably and rested. His skin softened into the colours of the rock around him. Somewhere outside, the ocean carried on with its busy evening. Inside the little den, all eight arms were finally ready for a quiet moment.

Fin loved mornings because the sea was full of voices. His dolphin pod clicked and whistled as they travelled together. Fin answered with his own familiar whistle, then leapt above the waves. Splash! He landed beside his aunt, who gave him a look that said she had not requested a shower. Fin was delighted anyway.

His aunt suggested a listening game. She sent clicks through the water and listened to the echoes returning from nearby objects. Fin tried it too. A rocky outcrop returned a different echo from a small fish. He could learn about things even when the water was too cloudy to see them clearly. It felt like a wonderful secret.

Fin tried clicking towards a patch of bubbles and listening to the returning sound. There was so much happening underwater that he sometimes had trouble deciding what to listen to first.
