His aunt made a whistle, and Fin turned towards her. A click could help him investigate his surroundings, while a familiar whistle could tell him something about his companions. Fin liked the idea that the ocean contained messages even where his eyes could see very little. He was determined to become an excellent listener, although for now he was mostly excellent at making noise.

Near a bend in the coast, Fin noticed how the pod's whistles carried through the water. His aunt reminded him to stay close and listen for familiar calls. Fin practised answering instead of making his loudest possible noise. “But my loudest noise is magnificent!” he said. His aunt smiled. “So is knowing when to be quiet.”

After lunch, the pod travelled through water stirred cloudy by the waves. Fin could barely see the dolphins beside him. A younger calf named Pip became nervous when his mother's shape disappeared in the murk. He whistled repeatedly, then began swimming in the wrong direction. Fin heard him and called to his aunt, who was swimming nearby.

Pip's whistle came again, shorter and more worried than before. Fin wanted to swim directly towards the sound, but the cloudy water made it difficult to see exactly where the little dolphin was heading. His aunt stayed close and gave a reassuring call. Fin listened for a reply. Somewhere beyond the murk was another familiar whistle, faint but clear enough to recognise. The morning game suddenly seemed very important. Could Fin help Pip listen for his mother's voice instead of swimming faster and faster in the wrong direction?

The aunt slowed down and gave a familiar whistle. Fin wanted to leap and splash to show Pip where they were, but remembered their morning game. Splashing would not make the water clearer. He stayed close to his aunt and listened. Soon they heard Pip's mother calling from the other side of the cloudy patch.

Fin's aunt guided the little group towards the mother's call. Fin kept answering gently so Pip could follow alongside them. As the water cleared, the calf spotted his mother and hurried to her side. She greeted him with a whistle and a gentle touch. Fin felt so happy that he almost forgot to breathe, then surfaced with an enormous puff.

Pip stayed close to his mother for a while, occasionally looking towards Fin and his aunt. The water was clearing now, and sunlight made long, wavering lines beneath the surface. Fin gave a small whistle, and Pip answered with one of his own. This time it sounded much more cheerful. They surfaced together, taking comfortable breaths before diving again. Fin felt rather proud, but the best part was not being the loudest dolphin in the sea. It was hearing the little calf's voice change from frightened to happy.

In the evening, the pod gathered in quieter water. Pip swam close to his mother while Fin told his aunt how worried he had been. “You listened before you acted,” she said. “That helped us find him.” Fin realised that his favourite trick, making a spectacular splash, had not been the right trick for every situation.

He practised the listening game once more. This time he waited for the returning echoes and the calls of his companions instead of rushing ahead. Pip joined in, making little clicks of his own. Fin imagined the sea as a great conversation, with room for every voice, even the smallest and quietest ones.

The dolphins moved through a brighter stretch of water. Fin heard a familiar whistle and waited before answering, giving the others a chance to call as well. Pip swam comfortably near his mother, practising the same listening game. A school of small fish flashed beneath them like scattered pieces of silver. Fin turned to watch, then remembered to stay with the pod. He had discovered that the sea was full of wonderful things to hear, and that listening to a friend could be just as interesting as discovering something new.

Under the fading sky, the dolphins travelled slowly together. Dolphins can rest part of their brain while remaining able to breathe, and Fin began to settle into the gentle rhythm of the pod. He heard his aunt's familiar whistle nearby. Tomorrow he would leap again. Tonight, listening to the voices he loved was adventure enough.

Pingo was very proud of his new game. He would take three little steps, flop onto his fluffy tummy and slide across the snow. “One, two, three, wheeee!” he squeaked. His father watched from among the emperor penguins. “Very graceful,” he said. “Especially the bit where you bumped into my feet.”

The Antarctic wind was chilly that morning. Pingo noticed that the grown-ups were standing so close together that he could hardly see the snow between them. At the outside of the group, birds shuffled slowly around. “Why don't they all go straight into the middle?” Pingo asked. “There isn't room for everybody there,” Father explained.

Pingo watched an adult penguin shuffle around the outside of the huddle. It did not push straight through the other birds. Instead, little movements gradually changed which penguins stood nearest the wind. The chicks near their parents looked quite comfortable. Pingo tried to imitate the grown-ups with a very serious shuffle of his own, but his feet were so small that he made hardly any progress. Pebble laughed. “You look like a fluffy little snow cloud.” Pingo decided he was a very distinguished snow cloud indeed.

Father showed him how the penguins changed places little by little. Those facing the wind would eventually reach a warmer spot. Pingo imagined a giant feathery blanket that could walk. He practised making a small gap beside his father, then closing it again. His tiny neighbour, a chick named Pebble, tried too.

After midday, the wind grew louder. Snowflakes swept sideways, and Pingo was glad to stand close to Father. But where was Pebble? He heard a thin, familiar peep from the edge of the group. There stood his friend, with fluffy feathers blowing in every direction. Pingo wanted to run straight over.

The wind lifted loose snow into the air until Pingo could barely see the little marks their feet had made earlier. Pebble was still close to the adult birds, but the gusts were making it difficult to hear one another. Pingo squeezed nearer to Father instead of running away from him. He watched the slowly moving group. He remembered how the grown-ups had made space without pushing. Perhaps, if he stayed near Father and waited for the next little movement, there would be a comfortable place for Pebble as well.

“Stay beside me,” Father said, answering the chick's call. Pingo remembered their morning game. There was a little space near his father's feet, but not enough for another chick. He stepped carefully sideways. Father shifted with him, and the neighbouring adults began to shuffle, each making a small adjustment for the next penguin.

Pebble slipped into the opening. “My toes were turning into icicles!” he exclaimed. Pingo giggled. “Mine are still penguin toes, I think.” They stood together while the adults continued their slow movement. When Pingo reached a warmer place, he didn't try to keep it forever. Another penguin needed it next.

The warmth of the group felt very different from standing in the wind. Pingo looked towards the outside and noticed another little chick with its feathers ruffled by the cold. The grown-ups continued shifting slowly, and Pingo moved with them rather than trying to hold his place. Pebble did the same. Neither chick had to be the strongest or the fastest. They simply stayed close to their parents and made room as the group moved. Soon both had warm toes, and Pingo's enormous worry had shrunk to the size of a snowflake.

Towards evening the snow stopped swirling. Beyond the huddle, the ice shone pale blue beneath the low Antarctic sun. Pebble thanked Pingo for making room. “But I only moved a tiny bit,” said Pingo. Father looked around the enormous colony. “A tiny bit from each of us makes a very big difference.”

Pingo tried his sliding game again on a small patch of soft snow. This time he waited until Pebble was ready. They slid side by side, two fluffy little bellies making two funny tracks. The adults called them back, and the chicks hurried towards the shelter of their familiar group.

When the little sliding game ended, Pingo looked back at their two trails in the snow. The marks curved towards each other, then disappeared beneath the feet of the penguins. Pebble gave a cheerful little peep. They tucked themselves near their parents again, where the cold wind was much less troublesome. Pingo decided that sliding was an excellent game, but sharing a warm place was an even better one. Perhaps tomorrow they could invent a new game, one that had room for all the little penguins.

At rest, Pingo nestled near Father. He could still hear the penguins calling softly, but the wind no longer seemed so fierce. He closed his eyes and pictured that enormous walking blanket. Its secret wasn't the warmest place in the middle; it was all the penguins looking after one another. Sleep well, little Pingo.

Nanu woke with a snowflake sitting on the end of his nose. He sneezed so loudly that his mother turned around. “A very impressive alarm clock,” she chuckled. He rolled onto his back and rubbed his thick fur in the snow. The Arctic morning was bright, and Nanu was eager to explore.

As he followed Mother, he noticed the enormous prints her paws left behind. His own broad paws were smaller but worked like snowshoes, spreading his weight over the snow. The fur beneath them helped him grip. He tried making a paw print shaped like a heart. It looked more like a squashed potato.

Nanu inspected his mother's footprints, then tried to put each of his smaller paws inside one of them. It was rather like walking along a row of enormous bowls. The broad paws helped him travel across the snowy ground, but Mother still watched carefully where she stepped. Snow could cover uneven surfaces, and conditions on the ice could change. Nanu looked up at a familiar ridge that stood out against the pale sky. He thought he could probably recognise it anywhere, although he had never seen it disappear behind a curtain of blowing snow.

Near a ridge, Mother paused to sniff the air. Nanu peered into a hollow protected from the wind. Inside, the snow was quiet and soft. “My snow castle!” he announced. Mother examined the place before they moved on. “Remember it,” she said. “A good explorer notices where to rest, not just where to go.”

By afternoon, clouds had covered the bright sky. Snow began to blow across their path. Nanu wanted to prove that he was a brave polar bear by racing ahead, but Mother stopped him. She listened, sniffed and looked for firm ground. Through the drifting snow, the familiar shapes had become difficult to recognise.

A gust swept across the ridge, and the outlines of the distant snowdrifts vanished. Nanu blinked, then tried to find the familiar shape again. His paws felt steady on the ground where Mother stood, but the landscape ahead was no longer clear. He had been imagining a splendid race across the white world, with his mother cheering behind him. Now he found himself wanting to stay close to her instead. Was stopping really part of being a strong polar bear? He watched her carefully, hoping to discover the answer.

Nanu spotted the ridge, with its little crooked top like a bear's ear. “The castle!” he called. Mother recognised it too and led him carefully towards the sheltered hollow. As soon as they stepped inside, the wind sounded much quieter. Nanu shook the snow from his ears, showering Mother with tiny white flakes.

“Are we giving up?” he asked, disappointed that their walk had stopped. “No,” Mother replied. “We're waiting for better conditions.” They rested together, and Nanu watched the snow stream over the ridge. He invented names for the shapes in the clouds until his eyelids grew heavy. Even a polar bear needed time to recover his energy.

The wind made little streams of snow curl around their sheltered place. Nanu watched one drift grow slowly against a rock. Mother rested beside him, keeping him close while conditions improved. Every now and then he lifted his nose and looked towards the ridge. The air was becoming clearer, but Mother was in no hurry. Nanu discovered that waiting did not feel quite so difficult when there were small changes to notice. At last the shape of the ridge appeared again, and he gave a very satisfied little grunt.

When the weather eased, Mother checked their surroundings again. The ridge was clear now, and the firm snowy ground stretched ahead. Nanu followed at her side instead of running. He spotted the earlier paw prints, almost filled with snow, and laughed at the little potato-shaped one. It was still recognisable.

They continued until they found another comfortable place to settle. Nanu felt proud, although he hadn't raced anywhere. “I thought being brave meant never stopping,” he admitted. Mother nudged his cheek. “Sometimes the wisest and bravest thing is knowing when to stop.” He tucked that thought away like a precious little stone.

Nanu looked back at the familiar snow shapes and the footprints they had left together. Some of the older marks had already been covered by drifting snow. He was glad they had not depended on those marks alone. Mother had chosen their route when the conditions were clearer, and he had learned by following her. His paws felt pleasantly tired now, not from a great race but from an ordinary journey made carefully. He leaned against Mother's warm fur. Tomorrow's adventure could begin when tomorrow was ready.

Evening brought a gentle blue light over the snow. Nanu curled beside Mother, his nose tucked beneath a furry paw. The wind whispered far beyond their resting place. In his dreams he was the king of a tiny snow castle, with one important royal rule: every explorer was allowed to rest.

Sami pushed his whiskery nose through an opening in the ice and took a splendid breath of cold Arctic air. “Pffff!” he blew, sending drops of water everywhere. His mother surfaced beside him. “Good morning, little fountain.” Sami grinned and disappeared beneath the water with a graceful twist.

Under the ice, the world was blue and quiet. Sami's whiskers were wonderfully sensitive to movements in the water. He practised following the little swirls left by Mother as she swam. Then she led him back to their breathing opening. A ridge of snow stood beside it, shaped rather like a crooked white hat.

Sami turned beneath the opening and saw a pale patch of light shining through the water above him. He rose beside Mother, breathed, and went back down for another short exploration. The snowy ridge looked quite different from underwater, but the opening was easy to recognise when he was close to it. “A little window to the sky,” he thought. He liked the way his whiskers noticed movements he could not immediately see. But no matter how interesting the world beneath the ice became, he would always need to come up for air.

“That's our window to the sky,” Sami decided. Seals are mammals, so even though they are excellent swimmers, they must return to air to breathe. Mother reminded him to stay close and surface regularly. They played near the opening, taking turns peeking above the water. Sami liked the way the sky appeared and disappeared.

In the afternoon, a shiny fish flickered past Sami's nose. It turned left, then right, then vanished behind a dark patch of ice. Sami started to follow, imagining the most magnificent fish supper ever. He was so interested that he nearly forgot the little game he had played with Mother.

The fish flashed once more, and Sami imagined himself catching the most wonderful dinner. Then it disappeared into the darker water. Sami could still sense little movements around him, but he could no longer see the pale patch of light as clearly. Mother was close, turning towards the place where they had surfaced before. Sami's excitement began to give way to a much more ordinary feeling: he wanted a breath. The fish might be very interesting, but it was certainly not important enough to forget the window to the sky.

He noticed Mother turning back towards their breathing place and remembered her lesson. The fish could wait. He followed her straight towards the familiar opening, where he surfaced and breathed comfortably. “There you are, sky!” he exclaimed. He rested for a while, watching snowflakes land on Mother's wet head and melt.

When they dived again, Sami stayed near Mother and paid attention to his own need for air. This time he discovered several fish without chasing the first one far away. His whiskers helped him sense their movements. One fish darted behind him, and Sami spun so quickly that he almost chased his own flipper.

When Sami surfaced again, he felt the cool air touch his nose. He gave a little puff of satisfaction. The fish had been quick, the water had been interesting, and he had still managed to take the breaks he needed. Mother rested nearby while he looked down through the opening. A silver shape flickered far below, but this time Sami did not immediately dive after it. He could go back when he was ready. For now he watched a tiny snowflake land on his whisker and vanish.

Later, Mother climbed onto a safe stretch of ice and Sami followed. Out of the water he was much less graceful, wriggling forward on his tummy. “I think someone has borrowed my beautiful swimming legs,” he joked. Mother settled beside him, and they watched the water move gently below.

Sami thought about the shiny fish. He had wanted to catch it very badly, yet he had enjoyed the afternoon much more when he remembered his breathing breaks. “The fish isn't in charge of my day,” he decided. “My body gets a vote too.” Mother gave him a soft, approving nudge.

Out on the ice, Sami listened to the gentle sounds of the water beneath them. He stretched one flipper and then the other, feeling the pleasant tiredness of an afternoon spent swimming. He imagined the little fish telling its friends about a seal who had been very interested in supper but even more interested in breathing. “A remarkably sensible seal,” he decided. Mother gave a soft sound beside him. Sami liked that there would be another chance to explore later, without needing to turn every interesting discovery into a race.

The evening sky grew darker above their resting place. Sami listened to the little splashes beneath the ice and felt his breathing become slow and easy. His next adventure could wait until another swim. He rested beside Mother, dreaming of a whole school of silver fish dancing under his window to the sky.

Bo woke up with a very serious problem: his stomach was making noises louder than his own growl. “I think there's a bear living in my tummy,” he announced. Mother laughed and led him through the autumn forest. Brown bears eat many different foods, and at this time of year they need plenty of energy before winter.

Near a fallen tree, Bo caught the delicious smell of ripe berries. The log was covered in green moss, with two little branches sticking up like ears. “A sleeping green bear!” he cried. Mother showed him the familiar berries she ate, and Bo carefully picked several of the ripe ones with his lips.

A leaf landed on Bo's nose while he was choosing a berry. He shook it away, then noticed a tiny beetle disappearing into the moss. The fallen tree was not simply a strange green shape beside their picnic. It was a home for little creatures, a place for moss to grow and a landmark he could recognise. Bo decided to remember its two little branch ears rather than trying to remember every tree in the forest. He could hardly believe how much was happening around a place he had only noticed because he was hungry.

A thrush fluttered onto a branch above them. Bo watched it swallow a berry and fly away. There was enough fruit for many visitors. Mother moved on to search for other food, and Bo memorised the mossy log. “Goodbye, green bear. Guard our picnic!” he said, trotting after her.

By afternoon, Bo's tummy was making its famous noise again. He hoped they could return to the berries, but the forest paths looked remarkably alike. A log lay across one path, another near a tree. None had two little mossy ears. Bo wanted to rush into the bushes to investigate every smell.

Bo sniffed at one log, then at another. Both smelled interesting, but neither was the green bear he remembered. The autumn forest seemed to have filled itself with confusing little paths. He felt impatient and wanted to follow every berry scent at once. Mother stayed close and let him take a moment to look. Bo remembered the big oak near the mossy log, and how the two branch ears had pointed towards the sky. There was no need to rush into unfamiliar bushes. Perhaps the forest would look less confusing if he noticed one detail at a time.

Mother waited while he stopped and looked. A familiar oak stood near the path, and beyond it he glimpsed the green log. “There!” he exclaimed. They approached the berry patch together. Bo was so pleased that he began munching enthusiastically, but noticed that some branches bent beneath his large paws.

He shifted onto a clear patch of ground and ate from the edge instead. A small bird landed on a branch nearby, looking for its own meal. Bo left the fruit on that side untouched. Mother found another ripe cluster, and they shared the peaceful picnic without flattening the bushes around them.

From the clear ground, Bo could reach the ripe fruit without stepping on the smaller branches. The thrush hopped closer to its own part of the bush, swallowed a berry and fluttered away again. Bo watched it with great interest. His own mouth could hold an enormous mouthful compared with the bird's little beak. They were sharing the same patch in very different ways. He found another delicious berry near the edge, and Mother moved on when they had eaten enough. Behind them the bush still stood, with plenty of fruit shining among its leaves.

As evening approached, the thrush returned with several other birds. Bo sat at a distance and watched them pluck the remaining berries. He realised the patch wasn't a secret cupboard made especially for him. It was part of a busy forest, where different creatures needed food for different reasons.

Mother and Bo continued towards their resting place, where dry leaves rustled beneath their paws. “Did I find the best picnic in the forest?” Bo asked. “You found a good one,” Mother smiled. “And you left it good for the next visitors.” Bo thought that sounded even better than being the best finder.

Bo looked back at the path and imagined the green bear guarding its picnic through the autumn. A bird called from the branches, and he thought of the little visitors who would be back after he had gone. He had discovered a good place to eat without needing to keep it all for himself. Mother walked beside him through the leaves, their paws making soft crunching sounds. Bo was already beginning to feel sleepy. The forest seemed like a very large home, with many different creatures making use of its corners in their own ways.

Under the darkening trees, Bo curled up with his warm fur against Mother. Soon winter would bring a long rest, but tonight was just an ordinary, lovely autumn night. His stomach gave one last tiny rumble. “Goodnight, tummy bear,” he whispered, and dreamed of a green mossy bear surrounded by birds.

Hazel was running a very unusual shop. It had no doors, no shelves and absolutely no customers. “One acorn for later, two acorns for later,” she sang, digging little holes in the soil. As a squirrel, she hid food in many places so she could find it when the weather turned colder.

Beside a heart-shaped stone, she buried a particularly round acorn. “That's my best one,” she declared, patting the soil flat. Then she scampered up an oak tree, using her bushy tail to help her balance along the branches. A gust of wind shook loose a shower of leaves around her.

Hazel stopped on a branch to admire her work from above. The heart-shaped stone was clearly visible between two roots, and she was quite sure she would never confuse it with another stone. She had hidden nuts in other places too, sniffing the ground and patting the soil after each little excavation. A squirrel's memory and sense of smell can both help it find buried food. Hazel took great pride in her collection. If only her pantry had been fitted with tiny wooden signs, she thought, everything would have been much easier.

Her neighbour, a young squirrel named Nutmeg, watched Hazel hopping from branch to branch. “Do you remember every hiding place?” he asked. “Of course!” Hazel replied, rather too confidently. Then she looked down at the forest floor. There were quite a lot of stones, roots and little holes. Perhaps remembering everything would be harder than she thought.

In the afternoon, a rain shower sent leaves tumbling across the ground. Hazel sheltered in the branches until the rain passed. When she came down, her carefully arranged little pantry looked entirely different. She searched for the heart-shaped stone, brushed away wet leaves and dug where she thought her best acorn was hiding.

The heart-shaped stone had become a nearly invisible lump beneath a blanket of wet leaves. Hazel brushed aside one leaf, then three more, until her paws were muddy. A stone appeared, but its shape looked more like a potato than a heart. She stared at it suspiciously. Had the rain moved her stone? Had she simply remembered the wrong root? She felt a little cross with herself. Her wonderful morning pantry no longer seemed quite so wonderfully organised. Somewhere nearby, Nutmeg was making his own small, careful searches.

She found an acorn, but it was smaller and pointier. Hazel tried another spot and found nothing at all. “My beautiful acorn has disappeared!” she cried. Nutmeg was collecting food nearby. He suggested looking around the oak instead of digging up every patch of soil in the forest. Hazel agreed to try.

Beneath the tree, she found several fresh acorns. She ate one and hid another in a different place. The missing one still bothered her, but she noticed a tiny oak seedling growing near an older hiding spot. Nutmeg explained that some forgotten nuts could germinate if the conditions were right.

Hazel crouched beside the tiny oak seedling. Two little leaves spread above the ground, looking wonderfully fresh after the rain. She tried to imagine an acorn sending its first root down into the soil. Some nuts would be found and eaten, of course, and others might never grow. But a few could become trees if they found suitable conditions. Hazel looked up at the great oak above her. It was hard to believe that something so enormous had once been so small. Her missing acorn did not seem quite so much like a disaster anymore.

As the evening light softened, Hazel looked again at the seedling. Perhaps her missing acorn might also become a little tree someday, if it escaped being eaten and had enough water and sunlight. She imagined a future oak with branches where young squirrels could play. Suddenly her mistake seemed a little less terrible.

Hazel collected one more fallen acorn before gathering her bedding. She hid it carefully in a different spot, then sniffed the ground around it. She still needed food for the colder days ahead, and she was not going to stop remembering her stores just because one had gone missing. But she did not feel quite so worried about being perfect. The little seedling stood beneath the tree, its leaves catching the last light. She looked towards her nest, carrying the thought of a future forest with her.

She made one last trip to collect soft leaves for her nest, carrying them carefully up the trunk. Nutmeg waved from another branch. “Did you find your treasure?” he called. “Not that one,” Hazel replied, “but I think I found a different sort of treasure.” She smiled at the little green seedling below.

Hazel settled into her nest of twigs and leaves, wrapped her bushy tail around herself and listened to droplets falling from the branches. Not everything had gone according to her plan, and that was all right. Sometimes a small mistake could lead to a lovely surprise. She fell asleep dreaming of an entire forest of future oak trees.

Luna stretched her paws and gave the smallest howl she could manage. “Awooo!” Her brother tried an even louder one, and they both collapsed into a giggling heap. Their wolf pack was a family, with grown-ups looking after the younger wolves. Today they were exploring a familiar stretch of forest together.

Near a rocky hill, Luna called again. A faint sound came back from the stones. “There is another Luna inside the hill!” she exclaimed. Her aunt explained that it was an echo. She demonstrated a longer call, and the sound returned, softer and less clear than the voice that had made it.

Luna tried another howl and listened as the rocky hill returned the end of it. The echo did not make a new sound of its own; it sent back part of the sound she had made. Her aunt called from a little distance away, and Luna noticed how different a familiar voice sounded. It could change its tune and call again even when Luna was silent. Her brother tried to persuade the hill to echo a particularly ridiculous squeak. The hill did its best, and both youngsters burst into a fit of giggles.

Luna listened as the adults called to one another from different parts of the trees. Wolves use howls to communicate over long distances. Each voice sounded a little different. Luna practised recognising her aunt's familiar call, and her brother made a silly squeak that sounded nothing like a proper wolf howl.

That afternoon, an interesting scent drifted from a bush beside the path. Luna stopped to sniff it, taking only a few little steps away. When she looked up, the pack had moved beyond the trees and she could no longer see them. She felt a sudden flutter in her stomach.

The trees suddenly looked much taller than they had a few moments earlier. Luna could still smell the path, but the familiar movement of her family was hidden beyond the trunks. A leaf scraped across the ground, and she turned towards it, hoping it was her brother. It was only a leaf. For one anxious moment she wanted to dash in every direction at once. Then she heard the wind moving past the rocky hill. The place was familiar. She remembered her aunt's voice and took a moment to listen instead of running.

She started to run, then stopped. The rocky hill was still close, and she remembered the familiar path beside it. Luna stayed near that spot and listened. At first she heard only the breeze. Then a long, clear howl rose from beyond the trees. It sounded exactly like her aunt, not like the echo from the hill.

Luna answered as loudly as she could. Her aunt called again, and soon came back along the path with another adult wolf. Luna hurried towards them. “I was trying to be a very independent explorer,” she admitted. Her aunt gently touched noses with her. “Independent explorers can still call for their family.”

Luna stayed close to her aunt as they returned to the others. When her brother appeared between two trees, he gave a delighted little howl. Luna answered, and this time she did not mind that her voice was slightly wobbly. The adults gathered around the young wolves, and the familiar forest seemed much less enormous. Her aunt explained that the pack could use calls to stay in touch, even when trees hid them from one another. Luna was glad she had answered. It was a very comforting thing to be heard.

The pack gathered at a quiet clearing as evening approached. Luna told her brother what had happened, and he promised to pay attention when they walked together. Their aunt invited them to practise calling and listening once more, this time from nearby places where the grown-ups could watch them.

Luna discovered that a howl wasn't just a splendid noise to make. It could tell someone where she was, reassure a family member or bring the pack together. She no longer felt embarrassed about asking for help. Her voice was a little piece of the family's connection, and she was glad to have it.

During their practice game, Luna waited until her aunt had finished calling before answering. Her brother tried a new howl, which sounded a little like a squeaky door, but Luna recognised him immediately. She was surprised by how much information a familiar voice could carry. As they rested in the clearing, she listened to the soft movement of the adults nearby. The forest was still full of mysterious sounds, yet the voices of her own family were wonderfully familiar. She decided that an explorer could be curious and careful at the same time.

Beneath the evening sky, Luna curled beside her brother in the shelter of the trees. The adults rested nearby. A distant call drifted through the forest, and her aunt answered softly. Luna closed her eyes, comforted by the familiar voices. Whatever adventures tomorrow brought, she knew she didn't have to face them alone.

While the sun was rising over the New Zealand forest, Kiri the kiwi was finishing her breakfast. She poked her long bill beneath a fern and found a juicy worm. “Delicious spaghetti!” she murmured. Unlike most birds, kiwis cannot fly, and many are most active at night. Kiri had been busy while the other birds slept.

She sniffed along the ground. Her nostrils were near the tip of her bill, which helped her locate food hidden beneath the leaves. A patch beside a big fern was especially soft and full of interesting smells.

Kiri examined the ground beneath the fern with her sensitive bill. The leaves were slightly damp, and she found a delicious little creature hiding beneath them. The forest floor was full of tiny trails that she could investigate with her sense of smell and touch. Above her, the early birds were already beginning their day, but Kiri had spent most of the night searching for food. She had no wish to race them into the sunshine. The big fern would still be here when she woke, she hoped, and she remembered where its fronds curved towards the ground.

Kiri remembered it before returning to the shelter where she rested during the day.

Outside, the morning birds started singing. Kiri tucked herself away and listened to their cheerful noise. “Good morning to you, goodnight to me,” she whispered. She could hear a little drip from a fern above her entrance. Soon she was fast asleep, dreaming of worms wearing tiny green hats.

In the afternoon, rain pattered through the forest. Kiri stirred when a heavy drop landed near her shelter, but stayed comfortably inside. The daytime birds hopped around in the wet branches, and the soft earth soaked up the rain. Kiri's favourite part of the day would come when the light faded.

The rain changed the sounds of the forest. Kiri could hear drops falling onto the leaves above her resting place, then dripping onto the ground. She was warm and dry enough inside, and she stayed where she was. At dusk, however, she would need to find food again. The fallen twigs might make her usual searching places look different. Kiri remembered the soft ground near the fern, where she had found breakfast before the daytime birds arrived. Perhaps the rain would make that little corner especially interesting tonight.

Near dusk, the rain slowed. Kiri woke and stretched her sturdy legs. She emerged into the damp forest and found the usual ground covered with fallen twigs. A young kiwi named Tui was probing a patch beneath a thick root, but the soil there was hard. He looked thoroughly disappointed.

Kiri remembered the fern she had visited at sunrise. She moved towards it and found the ground even softer after the rain. Tui searched a little distance away in the same patch, with plenty of space between them. His long bill disappeared beneath a leaf, and up came a wriggling supper. “Spaghetti!” Kiri exclaimed.

The fern was still standing, although its fronds were covered in shining drops. Kiri probed the damp ground and found another small creature beneath the leaves. Tui searched a comfortable distance away, and soon both young kiwis were busy with their own discoveries. There was no need to turn dinner into a competition. Kiri lifted her long bill and gave a pleased little sniff. The familiar patch had become even more interesting after the rain. A very ordinary place could hold a completely different surprise on another visit.

Evening turned into a quiet, starry night. Kiri continued along the forest floor, sniffing and probing in her own little territory. She found beetles and other small creatures beneath the damp leaves. When a branch rustled above her, she paused and listened before returning to her search. The forest was full of hidden treasures.

She thought about the little patch of earth beneath the fern. She hadn't needed to fly over the forest to find it, and she hadn't needed to search every corner at once. Paying attention to the small details around her had made her evening much easier. Tui had found his supper too.

Kiri travelled slowly through the dark forest, pausing whenever a promising scent reached her. She did not have wings that would carry her above the trees, but she had wonderfully useful senses for exploring the ground. She found a beetle beneath some leaves and listened to the night insects nearby. The rain had changed her usual route a little, and remembering the fern had helped her adjust. Now she was quite content to explore one small patch at a time. She was not in a hurry to discover the entire forest before morning.

As the night eventually gave way to another dawn, Kiri returned to her sheltered resting place. Her tummy was full, and the morning birds were beginning their songs again. “Goodnight, everyone. Or good morning. Oh, you know what I mean!” she whispered, closing her eyes for another peaceful daytime sleep.

Fen the fennec fox was the proud owner of two enormous ears. “One for listening to the left, and one for listening to the right,” he announced as he trotted across the Sahara sand at sunrise. His ears helped him detect tiny movements, and their large surface helped him release body heat.

Near the family burrow, Fen paused beside a rock that cast a little shadow. His furry feet helped protect his paws from the hot sand, but he knew the day would soon become much too warm for playing outside. He noticed that the ground near the rock stayed firmer than the loose sand around it.

Fen stood in the little patch of shade and listened. The desert seemed quiet until he stopped moving, and then he began to notice the wind brushing the sand and a faint scratching somewhere nearby. His enormous ears helped him hear such small sounds, as well as helping his body lose heat. He turned them towards the burrow, where Mother was calling him. The ground was already becoming warmer. Fen scampered towards the entrance he liked best, without giving much thought to the other opening on the far side of the familiar rock.

Mother called him underground, where the air felt cooler. Their burrow had several passages and openings. Fen liked one entrance best because he could pop through it like a cork from a bottle. “Why do we need the other one?” he asked. Mother smiled. “A home with more than one way out can be very useful.”

During the afternoon, wind swept across the desert above them. Fen woke briefly when sand whispered down the entrance to his favourite passage. Mother kept the young foxes resting in the cooler chamber. “Is the desert having a very large sneeze?” Fen wondered. His sister gave him a sleepy little yip.

Above the resting foxes, the wind moved loose sand from one place to another. Fen heard a gentle hiss at the mouth of the passage. When he opened his eyes, he could see a little pile of sand where the light usually appeared. Mother kept the young foxes inside the cooler burrow until the evening. Fen was not worried about the whole desert moving, but he did wonder whether his favourite doorway would still be easy to use. He thought about the other opening and the rock they had passed in the morning.

As dusk approached, Mother investigated the entrances. Loose sand had drifted across Fen's favourite opening. Fen was disappointed; he had been looking forward to his evening bounce. But Mother led the family through another familiar tunnel, emerging near the rock that Fen had noticed earlier. The air outside was finally cooler.

Fen stopped to listen. Beneath the sand, something made a faint scratching sound. He turned his ears, took a few delicate steps and began searching for an insect. His sister found another little creature nearby. Their evening meal was much easier to find when they were patient and quiet rather than bouncing everywhere.

Fen paused between the little patches of desert plants and turned his ears towards a faint sound. His sister noticed it too. They searched nearby without wandering far from their family. Above them, the sky was becoming a beautiful deep blue, and the sand was cooling. Fen's favourite entrance might still need time before it was comfortable to use again, but the other passage had allowed them to begin their evening normally. He decided it was rather nice to have another way home, especially in a place where the wind was always rearranging the sand.

The stars began to sparkle above the dunes. Fen looked back at the rock and the burrow's alternate entrance. If his family had depended on just one passage, the drifting sand would have caused more trouble. He imagined the foxes building a palace with a hundred doors, each with its own name.

“Perhaps one extra door is enough,” Mother laughed when he told her. Fen understood that being prepared didn't mean worrying about every possible surprise. It meant having sensible choices available. He and his sister explored close to the family, listening to the small sounds that other creatures might easily miss.

Fen looked up at the first stars and imagined a grand burrow with a hundred doors, all opening at once. Then he imagined trying to remember which one led to his favourite sleeping chamber. That sounded exhausting. He was glad the family had a familiar, useful alternative rather than a complicated palace. Mother knew the burrow well, and Fen was beginning to learn its shape too. When he was ready to rest, he would know exactly which entrance to use. The desert could keep making its little changes; he had learned to notice them.

Before the next sunrise, Fen returned to the burrow with his family. He settled into a cool chamber, folding his enormous ears comfortably against himself. Above them the desert waited for another hot day. Below, Fen dreamed of a palace with one hundred doors and a very polite wind that knocked before entering.

Nico was taking his final nighttime stroll when the first light appeared above the garden. He snuffled beneath a hedge, looking for beetles. A little gap between two roots led into a quiet corner of the garden. “A secret door!” he whispered, squeezing through before returning to his nest of dry leaves.

His spines were excellent protection, but they were not much use as a pillow. So Nico turned carefully in his sheltered nest until his soft underside rested against the leaves. He remembered the gap beneath the hedge, just in case he wanted to visit the garden again that night. Then he yawned.

Before going to sleep, Nico remembered the gap between the roots he had passed on his nighttime walk. The earth beneath the hedge was a little higher there, and a few dry leaves lay along the opening. He had sniffed it out while investigating the garden. It was not his usual path, but he could fit through it comfortably. He made a mental note, then wriggled deeper into his leafy nest. A hedgehog's busy night did not have to follow exactly the same route every time. There were plenty of interesting corners to discover.

A blackbird began to sing above him. Nico listened sleepily. Hedgehogs are mainly active at night, and he was ready for a long daytime rest. “Lovely song,” he murmured, “but perhaps a little quieter for your neighbour.” The blackbird did not understand a word, and Nico soon fell asleep anyway.

By afternoon, rain was dripping from the garden plants. Nico stayed warm beneath his shelter. Outside, a shallow puddle grew across his usual route, spreading from the path to a patch of grass.

The rain continued while Nico slept. Outside, the shallow puddle spread along the familiar path and covered some of the places where he usually looked for food. A leaf floated across it, turning slowly like a little boat. The higher ground beneath the hedge stayed much drier. Nico stirred inside his nest, listened to a particularly loud drip, and settled down again. He did not know that the little gap he had noticed in the morning would be rather useful when he began his next nighttime adventure.

When the sun began to set, the rain stopped, leaving little sparkling droplets on the hedge.

Nico woke hungry and emerged into the evening. He stopped when he reached the puddle. “Someone has installed a swimming pool!” he exclaimed. Rather than trying to push through the water, he remembered the little door between the roots. He turned back along the hedge and found the gap still open.

Beyond it, he discovered damp leaves and plenty of interesting smells. He found a beetle, then a worm, and had a very pleasant supper. Suddenly a branch rustled nearby. Nico curled into a protective ball. When the noise stopped and he felt safe, he uncurled slowly and peered into the darkness.

Nico listened for a moment, keeping his body still. He could hear the quiet snuffling of another creature coming along the hedge. The sound seemed familiar, but Nico waited until he could see what was approaching. He moved carefully into a comfortable little space beside the roots. A few drops fell from the leaves onto his spines, but the ground was firm beneath his feet. Nico was glad he had chosen the higher route instead of trying to force his way through the puddle. His evening had become pleasantly ordinary again.

Another hedgehog was approaching along the hedge. Nico moved aside to give it room, and the two continued in different directions. He was pleased that the little passage was wide enough for visitors to use without getting trapped. The garden seemed much larger now that he knew another route through it.

Nico wandered quietly through the garden, thinking about the puddle. His first path hadn't worked, but there had been no need to be upset or force his way through. He could simply look for a different solution. The secret door had turned a disappointing start into a delicious evening adventure.

The garden smelled fresh after the rain. Nico found another interesting patch of fallen leaves and searched beneath it with his nose close to the ground. Somewhere above, a branch moved in the breeze. He thought about his favourite old route, which had not been so useful tonight, and the leafy gap that had become his new favourite. He did not need to choose one forever. When the weather changed, he could notice what was different. The garden had plenty of little discoveries for a patient explorer with a very busy nose.

As the next morning approached, Nico returned to his leafy nest. The puddle was already smaller, but he chose the familiar dry route home. He tucked his nose into the soft leaves and settled comfortably. In his dreams, his little secret door had a tiny sign that said: There is often another way.

Once upon a time, in a make-believe tale set on Scotland's famous Loch Ness, Nessie lifted her long neck above the mist. “Bloop!” she greeted the morning. Loch Ness is a real, deep freshwater lake, but Nessie belongs to the world of legends and imagination. Today, in our story, she had a very important festival to watch.

The little village beside the water was preparing a celebration. Paper lanterns decorated the windows, and an imaginary water sprite named Misty was arranging floating flowers near the shore. One small enchanted lantern drifted towards a sheltered inlet. Nessie gently guided it into the calm water beside a crooked willow.

The enchanted lantern drifted towards a crooked willow whose branches hung low above the water. The misty surface reflected the lantern's little glow. Nessie lowered her head to admire it. In our imaginary loch, the lantern could float safely without a flame, and its light looked like a tiny star that had decided to go swimming. The sheltered inlet was easy to recognise from the shape of the willow. Nessie hoped the little star would still be shining when the festival began.

Misty fluttered over. “That lantern is for our evening dance!” she said. Nessie promised to remember the place. The sprite tied a blue ribbon to the willow in their magical story world, and the friends practised a little dance in the ripples. Nessie's version involved a tremendous amount of splashing.

By afternoon, a thick mist had rolled across the loch. The houses disappeared from view, and the little sprite could no longer see the familiar shoreline. Misty called from the reeds. Nessie heard her worried voice and swam towards it, staying in the sheltered part of the water. “Here I am,” she answered gently.

The mist wrapped itself around the loch until even Nessie's long neck seemed to disappear halfway up. Misty called again, and Nessie answered with a soft bloop. The little sprite's light was still glowing, but the familiar shapes of the village were hidden. Nessie did not want to hurry into the middle of the loch where it would be harder to find their way. She remembered the blue ribbon and the crooked willow, and she listened for Misty's voice. Perhaps the little sheltered place they had discovered that morning would be the right place to wait.

Misty was frightened that she would miss the dance. Nessie remembered the crooked willow and the enchanted lantern from the morning. She followed the familiar bank towards the inlet while Misty fluttered beside her. Through the grey mist, a faint golden light appeared, and the blue ribbon moved in the breeze.

They reached the sheltered inlet and stayed there while the mist began to thin. Misty was still worried, so Nessie told her about the time she had mistaken a floating log for another monster. The sprite laughed so hard that her wings made little circles in the water. Waiting felt much less frightening together.

Misty laughed at Nessie's story about the log, and her lantern made a tiny reflection on the quiet water. As they waited, the thick mist began to turn into thinner wisps. First they could see the willow branches, then the blue ribbon, and finally a faint glow from one of the village windows. Nessie did not hurry the little sprite. The festival would be much more enjoyable if Misty arrived feeling comfortable rather than frightened. The enchanted lantern was still shining, as steadily as it had that morning.

When evening came, the village lights became visible again. Misty carried her magical lantern towards the festival, and Nessie watched from the quiet inlet. The sprite's dance began, and the light reflected in the water like a little golden star. Nobody needed to know who had helped her find it.

Misty returned to thank her friend. “Your light wasn't very big,” Nessie told her, “but when everything was grey, it was exactly what we needed.” The sprite gave Nessie a little bow, and Nessie replied with a graceful splash that was not quite as graceful as she had intended.

The little sprite held up a small star-shaped charm made in their magical village. Nessie admired it and watched the festival lights appear one by one across the water. Misty had not needed an enormous lantern to find a familiar place, and she had not needed to face the grey afternoon alone. Nessie liked the thought of being a quiet friend who could help someone wait until the world became clearer. She settled near the inlet, watching the tiny lights dance on the water like a whole sky of swimming stars.

Under the stars, Nessie slipped into the peaceful loch of our imagination. A small circle of ripples spread across the water and disappeared. The village lanterns glowed softly. Sometimes a little kindness can be a light for someone who feels lost, Nessie thought, before settling into her secret, storybook sleep.

In our imaginary adventure high in the Himalayan mountains, Yeti stepped out of his cave and inspected the fresh snow. The Himalayas really do contain some of the world's highest mountains, but Yeti is a creature of legend. In this story, his feet were so enormous that a single footprint looked like a little bathtub.

He decided to make a snow face beside a great boulder. Two pebbles became eyes, and a bent twig became a smile. “Much better looking than me,” he declared. Behind the boulder was a sheltered cave, which Yeti knew well. The wind hardly reached inside, and the floor was dry and comfortable.

Yeti crouched beside the snow face and adjusted its twig smile. From behind the boulder, the wind was much softer, and the little cave felt pleasantly sheltered. He imagined himself running a mountain museum of funny snow faces. The first exhibit would have a nose made of snow; the second would have a spectacular moustache. He studied the large boulder carefully, because its shape was easy to recognise among the smaller rocks. Even on a snowy mountain in a magical story, it was useful to know where a comfortable shelter could be found.

An imaginary little mountain spirit named Pema arrived, laughing at the snow face. Together they made another one, much smaller, with a ridiculous snow moustache. Then they followed their familiar path, staying near Yeti's home. Pema liked collecting funny stories, and Yeti liked telling them in his deep, rumbling voice.

After midday, clouds drifted over the mountain. Snow began falling more heavily, and Pema could no longer see the distant rocks. The little spirit looked worried.

The distant peaks disappeared behind the falling snow. Pema looked towards the place where the little spirit's family usually appeared, but the familiar shapes were no longer visible. Yeti stopped making jokes for a moment. He knew Pema was not enjoying the game anymore. Instead of showing off how quickly his enormous feet could carry him, he looked for the nearby boulder. Its dark shape was still visible through the falling flakes. The little snow faces were probably being covered, but the sheltered cave behind them would be a much better place to wait.

Yeti stopped their game. He remembered the boulder and its sheltered cave, and led Pema back along the short, familiar path towards their morning snow faces.

The little moustache had almost disappeared beneath the new snow, but the huge boulder was still unmistakable. Inside the cave, the wind became a quiet whistle. Pema shivered. Yeti offered a soft bundle of imaginary mountain wool and sat nearby, leaving the little spirit plenty of comfortable space.

“Would you like a story?” he asked. Pema nodded. Yeti invented a tale about a mountain goat who wanted to become a snowflake and kept landing on his own nose. Pema laughed, and the two watched the snowfall from inside the shelter instead of trying to travel through it.

Yeti made the imaginary mountain goat's story even sillier. Every time the goat tried to become a snowflake, it landed in a different funny position, until Pema was laughing so hard that the little spirit forgot to be frightened for a moment. Outside the cave, the snow still fell, and they remained comfortably sheltered. Yeti listened when Pema wanted to talk and told another little joke when Pema wanted to laugh. The enormous mountain looked much friendlier from a safe place with somebody kind beside you.

Towards evening the snowfall eased, and the familiar path became visible again. In their magical mountain world, Pema's family appeared near the boulder to take the little spirit home. Yeti waved from the shelter. Pema gave him a tiny snowball shaped like a heart as a thank-you present.

Yeti looked at his enormous hands and feet. He had always thought those were the most impressive things about him. But the little spirit had needed a safe place, a patient friend and a funny story, not a giant display of strength. He placed the snowball beside his cave entrance.

Yeti admired the tiny heart-shaped snowball. It was not as large as his thumb, but he felt it was the finest treasure on the mountain. He looked towards the two nearly buried snow faces and decided to rebuild them on another clear day. Today he had discovered a new kind of adventure, one in which nobody needed to climb the highest peak or prove how strong they were. A warm shelter, a funny story and a little patience had made a very good afternoon. He listened to the mountain grow quiet.

The stars appeared over the snowy peaks. Yeti settled inside his cave and listened to the soft mountain wind. Being big could be useful, but being gentle was something even the smallest creature could practise. He smiled, closed his eyes and dreamed of two snow faces wearing the world's silliest moustaches.

In a make-believe forest in North America, Bigfoot woke beneath the enormous trees and stretched his enormous toes. Bigfoot is a legendary creature, not a confirmed animal, but in our story he was a very real friend to the imaginary woodland folk. His morning footsteps went stomp, squelch, stomp through the damp soil.

Beside a little stream, a fallen branch stretched from one bank towards the other. Bigfoot noticed how narrow and wobbly it was. A little farther along, his familiar woodland path crossed a broad, flat patch of ground beside the stream. There was a solid wooden footbridge there, made by the imaginary forest folk.

Bigfoot paused at the sturdy bridge and looked at the carved leaf on its post. It was a little oak leaf, with a wiggly stem and tiny lines cut into the wood. The imaginary forest folk had chosen it so travellers could recognise the crossing. Bigfoot put one enormous hand on the railing. It was much more reassuring than the narrow branch near the stream. He had no trouble remembering the path to the bridge, and he hoped the smaller woodland creatures would remember it too.

A tiny woodland sprite named Fern appeared and admired the branch. “It looks like a balancing beam!” she exclaimed. Bigfoot chuckled. “It looks like a way to get very wet feet.” They continued their morning walk, and Bigfoot pointed out the little bridge, with its two sturdy railings and a carved leaf on the post.

In the afternoon, rain fell over the forest. Water dripped from the branches, and the fallen limb became slippery. Fern returned to the stream, excited to visit her friend on the opposite bank. She thought the branch might be a quick way across, but stopped when she saw it wobble in the water.

The rain made the stream louder than it had been that morning. Fern watched the branch move against the bank and decided it did not look like such an excellent balancing beam after all. The sprite could see the other side of the stream, where a friend was waiting, but could not think of a safe way across. Fern called for Bigfoot among the dripping leaves, hoping he was nearby. There was no need to invent a dangerous shortcut when the forest folk had already made a proper bridge a little farther along the path.

Bigfoot heard her call and came along the path. He remembered the bridge with the carved leaf. “It takes a little longer,” he said, “but we don't have to turn ourselves into wet socks.” Fern laughed and followed him along the familiar path, well away from the slippery bank.

The bridge was just as sturdy as it had been in the morning. Fern crossed with Bigfoot beside her, holding the railing in their imaginary woodland world. On the other side her friend was waiting. Bigfoot gave them both a friendly wave and began walking back beneath the dripping trees.

The familiar carved leaf beside the bridge shone with drops of rain. Below them, the stream hurried between the banks, carrying little leaves and twigs away. From the bridge, it was rather lovely to watch. Behind him, the sprite and her friend were already talking happily. Bigfoot did not need to make a great leap or lift the branch out of the water. He had simply remembered a safe place and helped someone find it.

At sunset, Fern and her friend brought him a little picture they had drawn on a leaf. It showed an enormous footprint and two tiny ones, all leading towards the carved bridge. Bigfoot loved it. He hadn't expected a present or even a thank-you when he had offered to help.

He continued home, humming so softly that the woodland animals hardly noticed him. Somewhere in the distance, a hiker might have wondered about the huge footprints in the mud. But our story's Bigfoot was perfectly happy without being famous. Doing something kind had already made his day special.

On his way home, Bigfoot stopped beneath an enormous tree and admired the little picture on the leaf. The two small footprints looked rather funny next to the great big one. He traced the shape of the carved bridge with his finger. Nobody had watched his little adventure except Fern and her friend, and he was quite happy about that. A soft bird call came from the branches above, followed by the rustle of leaves. The forest was full of quiet things worth noticing, and Bigfoot liked being one of them.

The stream whispered beneath the evening sky. Bigfoot settled into his hidden forest home and placed the picture beside his bed of soft leaves. Kindness, he thought, didn't need an audience or a round of applause. It was enough to make somebody's journey a little easier. He closed his eyes and rested.

In a make-believe tale inspired by the Naga traditions of the Mekong region, a gentle serpent named Naga watched the morning sunlight dance across the river. The Mekong is real, and Naga figures hold important meanings in several cultures. Our particular Naga was an imaginary character who loved the colours of flowers and water.

The village in our story was preparing a little festival beside the river. Its imaginary helpers had made magical floating flowers for an evening display. Naga noticed several gathering in a sheltered inlet near a bend, where the water moved gently. A beautiful purple blossom spun slowly in a circle.

Naga watched the purple blossom turn beneath the willow-like branches near the bank. In this imaginary celebration, the flowers were enchanted decorations that the village helpers would collect again rather than leave in the river. The quiet inlet held the blossom while the main current moved swiftly past. Naga admired the different colours reflected on the water and remembered the shape of the sheltered bend. Mali was already busy preparing the festival, but the little flower had given both friends a reason to notice a place they might otherwise have passed.

A young festival sprite named Mali waved from the bank. “That is my favourite flower!” she called. Naga guided the magical blossom towards the sheltered edge. Together they admired the little inlet, where reeds swayed and the river seemed to take a quiet breath. Mali remembered its shape before returning to her preparations.

By afternoon, upstream rain had made the main river current stronger. Several of the magical festival flowers drifted away from their display. Mali looked upset. She wanted to hurry after them, but Naga reminded her that a powerful river deserved respect. Nobody should enter fast water to recover decorations.

The stronger current made the river look quite different from the gentle morning scene. Mali could see a cluster of magical flowers moving away, and for a moment the decorations seemed terribly important. Naga reminded her that the river was far more powerful than a floating blossom. The festival helpers remained on the safe path, looking for a place where the current would naturally carry the flowers into quieter water. Naga remembered the inlet and its spinning purple flower. There might be a way to recover the decorations without anybody going into the fast-moving river.

Naga remembered the inlet from the morning and suggested that Mali and the grown-up festival helpers follow the familiar path along the bank. From a safe spot, they could see a cluster of colourful magical blossoms gathering among the reeds. The purple one was there too, dancing in the gentle water.

The adult helpers recovered the decorations from the sheltered bank using their long festival baskets, while Mali stayed well away from the water's edge. Naga helped guide the enchanted flowers in our story world. Soon the baskets were full again, and Mali's favourite blossom rested safely on top like a little crown.

The adult helpers checked that the last enchanted flower had been collected. Mali clapped when the basket was brought back to the path. The decorations were a little damp, but that hardly mattered in a magical festival. They made sure none were left drifting away before returning to the village. Naga watched the reeds moving softly beside the inlet. The same river that had seemed so gentle in the morning had reminded everybody to pay attention, and they had found a way to celebrate while respecting it.

As evening arrived, the villagers arranged the decorations on the festival platform. Colourful lanterns glowed beside the river, and their reflections trembled in the water. Mali thanked Naga for helping everyone celebrate without taking unnecessary risks. Naga admired the lights quietly from the sheltered inlet.

The little sprite asked whether the river belonged to Naga. “No,” he answered in our tale. “We are all its neighbours.” They watched the water moving past the village. A river could be beautiful and powerful at the same time, and caring for it meant noticing what it needed as well as what people wanted.

Mali looked at the reflections of the lanterns and imagined the river flowing far beyond their little village, past other homes and forests. Naga listened to the water with her. They could enjoy its beauty without expecting it to do exactly what they wanted. The helpers would collect their festival decorations when the celebration ended, leaving the bank tidy for the next morning. Mali liked that idea. The beautiful little purple blossom could be a memory of the evening rather than something the river had to carry forever.

The moon rose over the Mekong. Naga slipped beneath the peaceful waters of our imagination, leaving the festival lights shining above. Mali waved from the safe path, and the village grew quiet. The river's gentle song seemed to remind everyone that respect and kindness help us share the world. Goodnight, Naga.

In the wide North American prairie of our make-believe adventure, Jackie the Jackalope bounced out of his cosy home. A jackalope is a legendary rabbit with antlers, not a real species. Jackie was especially proud of his imaginary antlers, although they had one annoying habit: they seemed to collect absolutely everything.

A dry leaf caught on one of the antlers. “A fashionable hat!” Jackie exclaimed. He hopped past a broad bush that cast a comfortable patch of shade over the ground. Beneath it, the air felt cooler. He paused for a moment, admired his leafy hat and memorised the little shady spot.

Jackie sat beneath the bush for a moment and admired the leaf balanced on his imaginary antlers. The shade was wonderfully comfortable, even though the morning was still fairly cool. He could hear the prairie grass whispering in the breeze and see tiny insects moving between the stems. “This is the Royal Resting Place of the Grand Wiggly Carrot,” he announced to nobody in particular. Then he bounced away, eager to find Juniper. He had no idea how useful a resting place might become in the middle of his favourite race.

His imaginary rabbit friend Juniper arrived, ready for their favourite hopping game. They took turns bouncing between familiar patches of grass. Jackie usually won because he was so enthusiastic, although Juniper was much better at choosing funny names for the finishing lines. Today's finish was called the Grand Wiggly Carrot.

By afternoon, the sun was much hotter. Jackie was ready for one more race, but Juniper began to slow down. “My paws feel tired,” she admitted. Jackie had almost reached the Grand Wiggly Carrot and wanted to finish first. Then he looked back and noticed that his friend was no longer smiling.

The finishing line was only a few hops away. Jackie could almost imagine the imaginary cheering crowd shouting his name. He glanced behind him, expecting Juniper to be laughing, but she had stopped. Her ears drooped a little, and the grass around them was no longer moving in a cool breeze. Jackie looked at the finish line again. Winning would take only a moment, but Juniper did not seem to be having fun anymore. He suddenly remembered the shady bush and his silly leafy hat. Perhaps the best part of the game was not the finish line after all.

He stopped the game immediately. “The carrot can wait,” he said. He remembered the broad bush from the morning and suggested resting in the shade. Juniper agreed, and they made their way to the familiar spot at a comfortable pace. Jackie sat beside her and gave her room to cool down.

They listened to the breeze moving through the grass. In their pretend prairie world, they had brought a little water flask for their outing, and Juniper took a refreshing drink. Jackie discovered another leaf on his antlers and presented it as a fancy parasol. Soon Juniper was laughing again.

Juniper took another comfortable sip and settled beneath the leaves. Jackie decided to make up a grand story about his very important antlers, which collected leaves because they were secretly trees. Juniper laughed and suggested that one of them might soon grow an apple. They stayed in the shade while the afternoon was hot, listening to the prairie sounds. There was no need to hurry back to the game. Jackie felt rather pleased when Juniper began smiling again, and he noticed that sitting together could be every bit as entertaining as racing.

When evening came and the air cooled, Juniper felt ready for a gentle game. This time Jackie asked what she wanted to play. They invented a slow-motion hopping contest, in which the funniest hop won instead of the fastest. Jackie performed such a dramatic wobble that both friends fell into fits of laughter.

At sunset they returned towards their homes together. “You could have won the race,” Juniper said. Jackie shook his antlers, sending the leafy hat fluttering away. “I think I won something better.” They had both enjoyed the day, and his friend hadn't needed to pretend she was comfortable when she wasn't.

They passed the Grand Wiggly Carrot on the way home, and Jackie gave the imaginary finish line a very grand bow. Juniper bowed too, then invented a new name for it: the Grand Wiggly Carrot That Could Wait. Jackie thought that was an excellent name. He no longer felt disappointed about the race they had stopped. They had found a better game and had enjoyed the evening together. Juniper picked up the leafy hat he had shaken loose and gave it back. Jackie wore it proudly for the rest of their walk.

Jackie tucked himself into his imaginary home and listened to the evening wind whispering across the prairie. A good friend notices when someone needs a break, he thought. He closed his eyes, dreaming of the Grand Wiggly Carrot and a whole collection of ridiculous leafy hats. Tomorrow, they could play again.

Sunny munches juicy pond grass by the sunny lake. The frogs sing a morning song, and a brave little bird lands on her back. Tickle, tickle! Up in the sky, puffy popcorn clouds float by. Rain is coming!
It’s getting hot! Sunny finds a cool, squishy mud puddle, all for herself. She closes her eyes and takes a nap. Plip, plop! Raindrops land on her nose. Nap over — and now she’s hungry again!
Under the big, bright moon, Sunny’s family munches together. Then — WHISTLE! Danger! Crocs are near! Clever Sunny leads everyone to hide in the mud. The crocs swim past. Safe! Goodnight, Sunny.
Did you know? Capybaras are the biggest rodents in the world!
Did you know? Capybaras can bark like a dog, purr when they’re happy, and whistle to call their family.
Did you know? Rolling in mud keeps capybaras cool, protects their skin from the sun and chases away bugs!
Did you know? Capybaras love big families, with lots of cousins and friends.
Echo the Hippo wakes up in the cool river. Only her eyes, ears and nose peek out of the water. Peek-a-boo!
Hippos don’t really swim — Echo walks and bounces along the bottom of the river. Boing, boing, boing!
When the sun goes down, Echo climbs out of the water to munch grass all night long. Munch, munch. Goodnight, Echo!
Did you know? Hippos spend most of the day in water to keep their skin cool.
Did you know? Hippos can close their ears and nose when they go under water!
Did you know? Hippos come out at night to eat grass.
Click the Tokay Gecko is sleepy. Geckos like Click rest in the daytime, hiding in a cozy crack in a big tree.
Click wakes up a little and licks his big orange eye to clean it. Tokay geckos have no moving eyelids to blink!
Night time is Click’s time! “To-kay! To-kay!” he calls, and climbs up the tree to look for crunchy bugs. Goodnight, Click!
Did you know? Tokay geckos are named after their loud call: “To-kay!”
Did you know? Tokay geckos can climb walls and even walk upside down with their special toes!
Did you know? Tokay geckos clean their eyes by licking them.
The sun tickles Mimi’s nose. She stretches her front paws… then her back paws… then she yawns a BIG yawn. Breakfast time!
Mimi finds a ball of red wool. Roll, pounce, roll, pounce! Oh no — now she’s all tangled up!
Mimi curls into a soft, round ball on the warm blanket. Purr… purr… Goodnight, Mimi.
Did you know? Cats often purr when they are relaxed, but they can also purr when worried or unwell.
Did you know? Cats sleep for most of the day!
Bruno wags his tail so fast his whole body wiggles. He brings his leash: “Walk? Walk? Walk?”
In the park Bruno digs a hole, finds a stick and gets mud on his nose. Splash — bath time!
Bruno lies by the door with his favourite sock. Snore… Goodnight, Bruno.
Did you know? Dogs use their very sensitive noses to discover scents that people cannot notice!
Did you know? Dogs wag their tails to show how they feel.
Rosa opens one eye, then the other. The grass is wet and shiny. Munch, munch!
Rosa swishes her tail at a buzzing fly. Swish! Swish! Go away, fly!
The sky turns pink. Rosa walks back to the warm barn. Moo… Goodnight, Rosa.
Did you know? Cows have best friends and feel calmer when they are together.
Pippo waddles out of his nest. Left foot, right foot — SPLASH! Into the pond.
Pippo dives: bottom up, head down! Bubbles everywhere!
Pippo tucks his head under his soft wing. Quack… Goodnight, Pippo.
Did you know? Ducks have water-resistant feathers that help keep their skin warm and dry!
Oli wakes up in a leafy nest, high, high up in the trees. Good morning, jungle!
Oli swings from branch to branch, looking for juicy fruit. Uh-oh, rain! Oli holds a big leaf like an umbrella.
Oli bends soft branches into a brand-new bed for the night. Goodnight, Oli!
Did you know? Orangutans usually build a fresh nest in the trees each night, and sometimes reuse one.
Did you know? An orangutan’s arms are longer than its legs — perfect for swinging.
Tiko stretches a long, long stretch and licks a big striped paw.
It’s hot! Tiko jumps into the river. Splash! Unlike many other cats, tigers are strong swimmers!
Tiko walks quietly through the shadows. The stripes make Tiko almost invisible. Goodnight, Tiko!
Did you know? No two tigers have the same stripes!
Did you know? Tigers love to swim — unlike most cats.
Kiki shakes her big, colourful beak and sings to the sunrise.
Kiki picks a berry, throws it up in the air… and catches it! Gulp!
Kiki turns her head, rests her beak on her back and folds her tail over like a blanket. Goodnight, Kiki!
Did you know? A toucan’s big beak is very light — it’s full of tiny air spaces inside!
Did you know? Toucans sleep with their beak on their back and their tail folded over it.
Ella fills her trunk at the waterhole and — WHOOSH! — gives herself a cool shower.
Ella throws dust and mud on her back. It’s like sunscreen for elephants!
Ella’s family walks home together, following the wise grandma elephant. Goodnight, Ella!
Did you know? An elephant uses its flexible trunk to pick up tiny leaves and move heavy branches!
Did you know? Elephant family groups are often led by an experienced older female.
Zuri stretches her long neck to the very top of the tree. The best leaves are up here!
Thirsty! Zuri spreads her long legs wide, wide, wide to reach the water.
The stars come out. Zuri hums a soft, low hum. Goodnight, Zuri!
Did you know? Giraffes are the tallest living land animals!
Did you know? A giraffe has a long, often dark-coloured tongue that helps it grasp leaves.
Ziggy and the herd munch fresh grass in the morning sun.
Ziggy and a friend nibble each other’s necks. Scratch, scratch — that’s how zebras say “I like you”!
The herd stays close together. Some zebras keep watch while the others rest. Goodnight, Ziggy!
Did you know? Every zebra has its own stripe pattern, like a fingerprint!
Did you know? Zebras are cousins of horses.
Tuga swims up, up, up to the top of the water and takes a big breath of air.
Tuga is a green sea turtle. She munches soft seagrass on the sea floor. Yum!
Tuga rests under a rocky ledge as the sea turns dark. Goodnight, Tuga!
Did you know? Sea turtles breathe air, so they swim to the top to take a breath. Adult green sea turtles mainly eat algae and seagrass.
Did you know? Baby sea turtles hatch on the beach and race to the sea!
Inky wakes up and changes from pale to dark and mottled! Good morning, colours!
Inky squeezes through a tiny hole. Octopuses have no bones, but their hard beak must fit through the opening!
Inky curls up in a cozy den made of shells. Goodnight, Inky!
Did you know? An octopus has eight arms and three hearts!
Did you know? Octopuses can change colour in a blink.
Fin jumps high out of the waves. Splash!
Fin whistles to the family. Bottlenose dolphins can have their own special whistle — a little like saying their name!
Fin sleeps with half of the brain at a time, so one eye stays a little open. Goodnight, Fin!
Did you know? Bottlenose dolphins have their own special whistles — a little like names!
Did you know? Dolphins sleep with half of their brain at a time.
Pingo waddles across the ice. Waddle, waddle, waddle!
Pingo flops on the belly and slides down the snow. Wheee!
Brrr, it’s cold! All the penguins huddle together to stay warm. Goodnight, Pingo!
Did you know? Penguins can’t fly, but they are super swimmers!
Did you know? Emperor penguin dads keep the egg warm on their feet!
Nanu rolls and rubs in the fresh snow to clean the thick white fur.
Nanu swims from one piece of ice to the next. Paddle, paddle!
Nanu curls up in the snow, nose under paw. Goodnight, Nanu!
Did you know? Under its white fur, a polar bear’s skin is black!
Did you know? Polar bears are great swimmers.
Sami pops up through a hole in the ice. Peek-a-boo!
Sami dives deep, deep down to look for fish. Hold your breath!
Sami rests on the ice under the dancing northern lights. Goodnight, Sami!
Did you know? Seals are mammals. They breathe air and can stay underwater for a long time.
Did you know? Baby harp seals are born with fluffy white fur.
